about_this_instance.heading: About this instance
about_this_instance.lede: What this Morphit instance claims about itself, so you can check.

error.fetch_failed: Couldn't fetch this instance's verification info.

error.suggestion: If this check fails on an instance you expected to be legitimate, try one of the known-good alternatives listed below.

field.branding_value: “{name}” — {count} files re-branded by this operator. The app code itself is unchanged, so the integrity check still covers it.

integrity.explain: verify.json, linked below, lists the {count, plural, one {# file} other {# files}} of this site's bundle, each with its hash — that list is the operator's own claim. The files that start the app (page shell, service worker, entry code) are also listed, with their hashes, in the latest release @morphit signed on the Blurt blockchain. When this site runs that signed version, your browser fetches each of those files from it and compares it with the signed hash. That catches a file changed by accident, by a partial break-in or on its way to you. It cannot protect you from the operator itself, who serves this check too.
integrity.check_mismatch: Only {matched} of {total} signed files match release {version} — this site serves changed files
integrity.check_not_checked: Not checked: this site runs version {running}, the latest signed release is {version}
integrity.check_no_release: Not checked: the signed release could not be read
integrity.check_incomplete: Not completed: a signed file could not be read from this site
integrity.check_unconfirmed: Not checked: the newest signed release could not be confirmed (the only one read is version {version}, older than this site's {running}). Checked again within the hour.

asset_stance.explain: Morphit is a federated marketplace. Every operator chooses which tradable assets their instance accepts new orders for — the default is everything in the canonical registry, but an operator can disable any trade-only asset (e.g. USDT) if they prefer their instance to specialize in privacy-first or decentralization-first assets. This is YOUR instance's current stance. Federation note: orders posted on other instances still appear in your orderbook regardless — the gate is only on new orders posted FROM here.
asset_stance.disabled_none: None — this instance accepts every tradable asset.
asset_stance.disabled_suffix: (operator-disabled on this instance; tradeable on peer instances)
asset_stance.federation_note: Want a different stance? Browse /operators to find an instance whose policy matches your preference, or run your own — see /run-a-node.

worried.explain: Morphit is federated — anyone can stand up an instance. If this one seems off, move to one you trust. Your keys, orders, and reputation live on the underlying chain, not on any single instance. You will see the same marketplace from anywhere.
worried.faq_pointer: For more on how to spot a bad operator, see
worried.compare_tool_pointer: If you want to compare what this instance shows against another, try the
worried.type_warning_heading: Type these into your browser bar — don't click
worried.type_warning_body: If you suspect this instance is rogue, the links here can't be trusted either — a hostile instance can render visible text saying "morphit.io" while the underlying URL points elsewhere. Type the addresses by hand into a clean browser tab.

payment_stance.explain: Every operator also chooses which payment methods their instance offers. The default is every method in the canonical registry; an operator can turn off any of them — most often Barter (goods/services) — to keep their instance money-only or focused. This is YOUR instance's current stance. Federation note: orders from other instances that use a disabled method still appear in your orderbook; the gate is only on new orders posted from here.
payment_stance.disabled_none: None — this instance offers every payment method.
payment_stance.disabled_suffix: (operator-disabled on this instance; usable on peer instances)

about_this_instance.fee_recipient_unregistered: This instance's fees account @{account} is not in its operator's on-chain registration yet, so other instances in the federation hide orders paid in BLURT here and do not deliver first messages sent from here to their users. The operator fixes this by running sudo morphit-ops register on the server.

setup_wizard.heading: Configure your instance
setup_wizard.intro: This wizard helps you generate the configuration lines and CLI commands you need to customize this Morphit instance. Nothing on this page mutates your server — you'll copy the output into your morphit.env file or your terminal, then restart your services.

assets.heading: Listed assets
assets.intro: Choose which crypto assets your instance lists for trading. BTC, XMR, and BLURT are always enabled — federation depends on them.
assets.output_heading: Add this line to your morphit.env file
assets.output_subtitle: Then restart the indexer service: `docker compose restart indexer`
assets.locked_title: Federation depends on this asset — operators cannot disable it

payment.heading: Add a custom payment method
payment.intro: If your region uses a payment method we haven't added to the canonical list, you can publish it as an instance-specific addition. Other instances will see it labeled with this instance's name.
payment.key_help: Lowercase letters, digits, underscores only. Maximum 32 characters. This is permanent once broadcast — orders will reference it forever.
payment.key_error_format: Lowercase letters, digits, and underscores only
payment.key_error_reserved: Key collides with a canonical method — pick a different key
payment.name_help: The user-facing name. Usually a brand name — don't translate it.
payment.description_help: One or two sentences. Users see this when choosing payment methods.
payment.output_heading: Run this command on your server
payment.output_subtitle: From the directory where you installed Morphit, paste this into your terminal. You'll be prompted for the posting key file path.
payment.output_pending: Fill in the key, name, description, and category fields above to generate the command.
payment.remove_key_error_canonical: Canonical methods can't be removed via the per-instance mechanism

disclosure.heading: What this wizard does and does not do
disclosure.read_only: Read-only: this page generates config and CLI text but never mutates your server. Nothing changes until you paste the output and apply it yourself.
disclosure.no_auth: Open access: this page has no login requirement because it never mutates anything. Anyone can visit it. If that's not what you want, place it behind your reverse proxy's auth.
disclosure.restart_required: Service restart required: after editing morphit.env, restart the indexer service so the change takes effect. The payment-method CLI broadcasts to chain immediately — no restart needed for that.

payment_remove.heading: Remove a custom payment method
payment_remove.intro: If you previously added a payment method via the CLI and want to retire it, generate the remove command here. Canonical methods (PayPal, Wise, etc.) cannot be removed — they're project-wide.
payment_remove.key_help: The exact key you used when adding the method. Run `morphit-ops payment-method list` on your server to see your current additions.
payment_remove.output_heading: Run this command on your server
payment_remove.output_subtitle: From the directory where you installed Morphit. You'll be prompted to confirm before the chain op is broadcast.
payment_remove.output_pending: Enter the machine key of an instance-specific method to generate the remove command.
payment_remove.orders_safety: Existing orders that reference this method continue to display correctly after removal — the on-chain key persists in those orders' history. Remove just means new orders can't pick it.

payment_disable.heading: Offered payment methods
payment_disable.intro: Choose which payment methods your instance offers. Unchecking a method hides it from the post-order picker and the orderbook filter. Disabling Barter (goods/services) is the common case — some operators keep their instance money-only.

app.tagline: Buy and sell crypto, your way.

privacy_warnings.usdt_centralized: Two things to know about USDT before trading: Tether Inc. issues and administers USDT and has the technical ability to freeze addresses (and has used it). Transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BNB Smart Chain) — a property of those chains. Pick the asset that fits your trade.
privacy_warnings.usdc_centralized: Two things to know about USDC before trading: Circle issues and administers USDC and has the technical ability to freeze addresses (and has used it). Transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon) — a property of those chains. Pick the asset that fits your trade.
privacy_warnings.dai_partly_centralized: Three things to know about DAI before trading: (1) Unlike USDT and USDC, DAI's token contract has no admin-controlled freeze function — MakerDAO can't blacklist your address. This is a real decentralization advantage. (2) DAI is partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module, so Circle's freeze power over USDC indirectly affects DAI redemption when the PSM holds USDC. (3) Like all stablecoins, DAI transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum) — a property of those chains, no on-chain privacy. Pick the asset that fits your trade.

avatar_menu.backup_nudge_aria: Action needed: back up your keys

avatar_menu.backup_pending_aria: You have keys that are not backed up yet

backup_keys.title: Back up your keys
backup_keys.subtitle: This is the most important page on {brand}. Read it before you need it.
backup_keys.reality_lead: Morphit is non-custodial. Nobody — not us, not your operator, not any support agent anywhere — can help you recover your account if you lose your keys.
backup_keys.reality_body:
There is no 'forgot password' link. There is no 'verify with ID' process. There is no backup account on a server somewhere. Your keys exist in two places: this device (right now) and wherever you copy them to. That's the entire list.

Lose the keys, lose the account. Lose the funds. Lose the reputation you built from every trade. No exceptions, no appeals, no human on Earth can intervene.

This is the tradeoff for a service that does not, and cannot, seize your money or freeze your account. The same thing that keeps you safe from us keeps you exposed to your own mistakes.
backup_keys.reality_slogan: In the crypto world, YOU are the bank.
backup_keys.what_heading: What to back up, and how
backup_keys.seed_body:
Your seed phrase is a standard BIP-39 list of 12 words, generated during onboarding. Morphit turns it into your Blurt keys with its own published derivation step, so another BIP-39 wallet given the same words will NOT produce these keys: only Morphit (or another program that implements the same open-source derivation) can regenerate them. To use your account in another Blurt wallet, back up your WIF keys as well. The seed is your ultimate recovery inside Morphit.

If you didn't write it down during onboarding, it's gone. We cannot regenerate it. Your keys were derived from it before it was wiped from memory.
backup_keys.seed_tip_paper: Write it on paper. Two copies, stored in two separate physical locations.
backup_keys.seed_tip_steel: For amounts you care about, stamp it into a steel backup plate. Paper burns and gets waterlogged.
backup_keys.seed_tip_split: For larger balances, split it: first 6 words in one location, last 6 in another. Both halves together = full access. Neither half alone = nothing.
backup_keys.seed_tip_digital_warning: Never store the seed in email, cloud notes, screenshots, password managers synced to a cloud, or any app that can be remotely accessed.
backup_keys.keyfile_body: This keyfile is your private keys, encrypted with your device password. Download it now and store it somewhere separate from the device you're using. If you forget the password, the keyfile is useless — so treat the password as equally critical.
backup_keys.keyfile_locked_hint: Sign in first to download your encrypted keyfile. This page still works without signing in for the education.
backup_keys.keyfile_download_err_locked: Your session appears to be locked. Sign in to download your keyfile.
backup_keys.redundancy_body:
The crypto survivors are the ones who planned for fire, flood, death, and their own forgetfulness.

Two physical copies of your seed phrase in separate locations. At least one in a safe or safety deposit box. Consider an estate plan: how does a trusted heir find your keys if something happens to you? Write down the instructions separately from the keys themselves.

Redundancy costs you 10 minutes of effort. Its absence can cost you everything.
backup_keys.keyfile_body_posting_only: This keyfile is your private posting key, encrypted with your device password. Download it now and store it somewhere separate from the device you're using. If you forget the password, the keyfile is useless — so treat the password as equally critical.
backup_keys.redundancy_body_posting_only:
The crypto survivors are the ones who planned for fire, flood, death, and their own forgetfulness.

Two encrypted copies of your keyfile, kept in separate physical locations. At least one in a safe or safety deposit box. Consider an estate plan: how does a trusted heir reach your funds if something happens to you? Write down the instructions separately from the key itself.

Redundancy costs you 10 minutes of effort. Its absence can cost you everything.
backup_keys.antipatterns_heading: Common mistakes that cost people everything
backup_keys.anti_email: Emailing the seed phrase to yourself. Any breach of your email provider exposes it.
backup_keys.anti_cloud: Storing the seed in Google Drive, iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive. These are searched by automated malware, subpoenaed by governments, breached by attackers.
backup_keys.anti_photo: Taking a photo of the seed. Your photos sync to the cloud. Your phone gets stolen. The photo leaks.
backup_keys.anti_share: Sharing the seed with 'support' — ours, or anyone else's. Real support never, ever asks for your seed. Anyone who does is a scammer.
backup_keys.anti_support: Assuming someone can help you recover. They can't. We can't. Nobody can. This is the whole point of non-custodial.
backup_keys.faq_lost_keys: What happens if I lose my keys?
backup_keys.error_download_failed: Couldn't prepare your keyfile for download. Try again.

show_seed.heading: Show me my 12-word seed phrase
show_seed.body: If you didn't write your seed phrase down at sign-up, you can recover it here. We'll ask for your password before showing it.
show_seed.password_hint: Same password you use to unlock {brand} on this device.
show_seed.shoulder_warning: Make sure nobody is looking at your screen.
show_seed.locked_hint: Sign in first to view your seed phrase.

error.locked: You need to be signed in to view your seed phrase.
error.no_seed_posting_only: This account was imported with a posting key only — there's no seed phrase to show. Use the keyfile download below for backup.
error.no_seed_posting_active: There's no 12-word seed for this account, and there can't be. A seed derives your keys — it can't be built backwards from keys you already had. Your keyfile below is your backup, and it now contains both your Posting and Active keys.

paired.heading: Your keys live on your phone
paired.body: This desktop is paired with your phone, which holds your real keys. The sections below are about backing up keys that aren't on this device — they apply to the phone you paired with. Open {brand} on the phone and go to "Back up my keys" there.
paired.deeplink_hint: If your phone is nearby, the button below opens the right page on it directly.

backup_keys.keyfile_body_posting_active: Your keyfile now holds your Posting key AND your Active key, encrypted with your {brand} password. Keep a copy somewhere safe: it's the only backup of the Active key you just saved to this device. It does not contain your Owner or Memo keys — those stay wherever you keep them today.

set_password.heading: First, choose a password for your backups
set_password.body: You signed in with your seed phrase just for this session, so your keys are locked in this browser under a random password you have never seen. A keyfile made from that would not open with anything you know. Choose a password: your keyfile and “Show my seed” will use it. Nothing is saved to this device.
set_password.error_mismatch: The two passwords are not the same.
set_password.error_weak: That password is too weak. Use at least 12 characters.

message.placeholder_encrypted_paired: Encrypted message — open {brand} on your phone to read it.
message.placeholder_encrypted_failed: This message couldn't be decrypted on this device. It may be damaged or sent to a different recipient key.
message.peer_not_ready: This recipient hasn't opened Morphit chat yet. Once they do, your message will go through on retry.
message.not_confirmed_on_chain: Not confirmed on the blockchain — it may have been dropped. Tap Retry to send it again.
message.on_chain_not_accepted: On the blockchain, but not accepted for delivery — the recipient may not be taking messages from you right now. Sending it again would not change that.
message.session_locked: Your session is locked. Unlock and try again.
message.unrecorded_detail: This message reached you directly from the sender's server, but the blockchain never recorded it, so there is no permanent proof it was sent. If the sender's app reported it as not sent, they may send it again.
message.unrecorded_detail_own: This message was sent from another of your sessions, but the blockchain never recorded it, so there is no permanent proof it was sent. You can send it again.
message.sender_unverified: Sender not verified: this message came in an older format (or after a key change you haven't accepted), so it can't be proved that this person wrote it. Don't pay to an address in it without confirming it with them another way.

composer.locked_hint: Unlock your session to send messages.

acct_reminder.heading: Permanent.
acct_reminder.body: Account numbers in chat go on the blockchain forever. Proofread carefully before sending.

inbox.empty_body: Find a trader on the orderbook or a profile page and tap Message to start a conversation.

block.body: They will no longer be able to message you on Morphit. You can unblock them later from Settings.

stranger_fee.heading: Send your first message to @{peer}
stranger_fee.explain: {brand} charges a small one-time fee for first-contact messages to new people. This discourages spam while letting real conversations start freely.
stranger_fee.one_time_note: You'll never be charged again for messaging @{peer}. The fee only applies to the first message between two people.
stranger_fee.pill_explain: You haven't messaged @{peer} before. A small one-time fee unlocks this conversation.
stranger_fee.pill_locked_hint: Unlock your session to pay and send.

error.quote_failed: Could not fetch the current network fee. Please check your connection and try again.
error.no_active_envelope: No saved active key found on this device. Save your keys from Settings first, then try again.
error.broadcast_failed: Payment could not be broadcast. Your fee has not been spent. Please try again.
error.bad_password: That password did not unlock the active key.

escalation.heading: Fee escalated to {multiplier}× — you've messaged {count} stranger(s) in the last {window} minutes.
escalation.body: Please slow down. People dislike unsolicited contact and may block you. Wait at least 5 minutes between first contacts and the fee goes back to the base price.

security.pub_pin_tampered_same_ref: We couldn't safely send: this peer's chat-key record looks tampered. The chat key your indexer is reporting doesn't match what was published on-chain. Try a different Morphit instance, or ask the recipient to confirm their chat key out of band.
security.pub_pin_older_indexer_ref: We couldn't safely send: your indexer is reporting a chat-key record that's older than what you've already seen. That shouldn't happen on a forward-only chain. Try refreshing or switching to another Morphit instance.
security.pub_pin_chain_reports_none: We couldn't safely send: your indexer says this peer has a chat key, but the blockchain reports none. The indexer may be out of sync, or fabricating data. Try another Morphit instance, or wait and retry.
security.pub_pin_chain_older_than_pin: We couldn't safely send: the blockchain reports an older chat key for this peer than the one you've already seen. That's internally inconsistent. Try another Morphit instance or another blockchain endpoint.
security.pub_pin_malformed_indexer_response: We couldn't safely send: your indexer returned malformed data for this peer's chat-key record. The indexer may be running an older version or be misconfigured. Try another Morphit instance.

confirm.title: Chat Security
confirm.body: Do you want to stop being able to reread your own messages after you leave this chat? Your partner can still read them, and their encrypted form stays on the chain. Choose No to keep reading your own history, like a normal messenger.
confirm.current_keep: Right now: you keep a copy and can reread your own messages.
confirm.current_destroy: Right now: you don't keep a copy, so you can't reread your own messages after you leave.

pdf_reminder.title: Don't forget to export this chat to PDF
pdf_reminder.body: In this mode you can't reread your own messages after you leave (your partner still can). Save a PDF now if you want to keep a copy.

security.chain_unreachable: We couldn't reach the blockchain to check this peer's chat key, so the message wasn't sent. This is common on Tor and I2P, where connections take a while to build. Nothing is wrong — try again in a moment.
security.pub_pin_key_changed: Not sent: this person's chat key changed. That happens when they reset their keys — or when someone is trying to read your messages. Open ⋮ → Verify peer and compare the new safety number with them over another channel before you accept it.
security.accept_new_key: I compared it — accept the new key

chat.lazy_load_failed: Couldn't load the chat view. Refresh the page and try again.

address.address_invalid_btc: That doesn't look like a valid Bitcoin address.

address.amount_invalid: Enter a positive number, no units.
address.note_placeholder: For example: cash in hand at 3pm

address.memo_explain: The buyer must include this memo in their BLURT transfer so you can match the payment to this trade.
address.memo_required_explain: Paste this memo into the memo field of your BLURT transfer. Without it, the seller can't match your payment to this trade.
address.xmr_jitter_explain: Adds a tiny random amount (less than ~$0.0002) to make this transfer unique on Monero's chain. Defeats 'same-amount' correlation attacks. Recommended.
address.send_failed: Couldn't send the address. Try again.
address.xmr_jitter_send_exact_hint: Tell your buyer's wallet to send this exact amount, including the long decimals.
address.xmr_jitter_off_warning_body: Round amounts are easier to correlate on the Monero chain. Leave jitter on unless you have a reason to send an exact figure.
address.address_placeholder_usdt: Tether address (matching the network you picked)
address.address_invalid_usdt: This address does not match the USDT network you picked. Double-check before sending — cross-network sends lose your funds.
address.address_invalid_bch: That doesn't look like a valid Bitcoin Cash address.
address.address_invalid_ltc: That doesn't look like a valid Litecoin address.
address.amount_jitter_explain: Adds a tiny random extra (small enough to be a trivial implicit tip) to defeat amount-correlation between your order and the on-chain transfer. Strongly recommended on transparent chains.
address.amount_jitter_will_send: Your buyer's wallet will send exactly:
address.amount_jitter_send_exact_hint: This precise amount breaks the link between your order book post and the on-chain payment.
address.amount_jitter_off_warning_body: Anyone watching the chain can match this exact amount to your order. Turn the randomizer on unless you have a specific reason not to.
address.reuse_warning_body: You shared this address from this device before. Reusing the same address across trades links them on the public chain. Consider deriving a fresh address from your wallet for this trade.
address.payjoin_explain: If your wallet supports PayJoin (BIP-78), paste its endpoint URL here. Buyers whose wallets also support PayJoin will use a cooperative transaction that breaks chain-analysis heuristics. No effect on wallets without PayJoin support.
address.payjoin_badge_tooltip: The seller's wallet supports PayJoin (BIP-78). If your wallet supports it too, opening this URI will negotiate a cooperative transaction that improves privacy.
address.address_invalid_dash: That doesn't look like a valid Dash address.
address.address_placeholder_usdc: USD Coin address (matching the network you picked)
address.address_invalid_usdc: This address does not match the USDC network you picked. Double-check before sending — cross-network sends lose your funds. Note that Ethereum, Base, and Polygon addresses all start with 0x and look identical at the format level.
address.address_invalid_dai: Not a valid DAI address shape (expected EVM 0x[40 hex]).
address.address_invalid_doge: That doesn't look like a valid Dogecoin address.
address.address_invalid_zec: That doesn't look like a valid Zcash address.

address.address_invalid_xrp: Not a valid XRP Ledger address.  Expected an address starting with r followed by 24-34 base58 characters (no destination tag in this field).
address.blurt_account_not_found: No Blurt account with that name exists.

funds_sent.modal_subtitle: @{peer} will see the amount and transaction ID you enter below.
funds_sent.txid_help: The unique fingerprint your wallet showed after sending. Most wallets call it a TxID, Transaction Hash, or Tx Hash. It looks like a long jumble of letters and numbers (64 characters). Tap any sent transaction in your wallet to find it.
funds_sent.txid_invalid: That doesn't look like a valid transaction ID.

funds_sent.verify_mismatch_from: The transfer was sent from a different account than the buyer claims.
funds_sent.verify_mismatch_amount: The on-chain amount differs from the amount you asked for.
funds_sent.verify_mismatch_memo: The on-chain memo doesn't match the requested memo.

funds_sent.self_verify_mismatch_from: The on-chain transfer's sender doesn't match your account.
funds_sent.self_verify_mismatch_amount: Your wallet sent a different amount than expected.

section_identity.heading: Account name vs seed phrase vs password
section_identity.account_name_body: Your public name on the chain (e.g. @alice). Other people see this. Choosing a new one is permanent — costs ~3 BLURT.
section_identity.seed_phrase_body: 12 words. The ONLY way back into your account if you lose your device. Anyone who has them owns your account. Write them on paper, store somewhere safe.
section_identity.password_body: Just for THIS device, not the chain. Encrypts your seed in this browser. If you forget it, type your seed phrase to log in again. Different from the seed.

section_fees.heading: Listing fee vs network fee vs trade payment
section_fees.listing_fee_body: What {brand} charges to publish your order. Tiny — about 12.5¢ (USD-equivalent) if you pay in BLURT, or about 25¢ if you pay in BTC or XMR. Your first buy is free (an order worth at least $1). You enter amounts in your own currency — you never have to think in BLURT.
section_fees.network_fee_body: What the Bitcoin or Monero network charges to confirm a payment. Goes to miners, not {brand}. Varies — check the wallet you send from.
section_fees.trade_payment_body: The actual money you send (or receive) for the trade. {brand} never holds it — straight from buyer to seller, off-platform.

section_assets.heading: Supported tradable assets
section_assets.btc: Bitcoin. Most known. Public ledger — anyone can see who paid whom. Fees vary widely.
section_assets.xmr: Monero. Private — no one can see who paid whom. Fees usually low. The privacy choice.
section_assets.blurt: The token of the Blurt blockchain that {brand} runs on. Used to pay listing fees, post messages, sign orders.
section_assets.usdt: Tether stablecoin. Pegged 1:1 to USD. Trade across four networks: ERC-20 (Ethereum), TRC-20 (Tron), SPL (Solana), BEP-20 (BNB Smart Chain). Pick the network before sending — cross-network is unrecoverable.
section_assets.bch: BCH — Bitcoin Cash, transparent, decentralized, bigger blocks than BTC
section_assets.ltc: LTC — Litecoin, fast, low-fee Bitcoin fork (since 2011). Trade-only on {brand}. Use a Litecoin wallet (Electrum-LTC, Litewallet, hardware wallets); accepts L… legacy, M… modern P2SH, and ltc1… SegWit addresses.
section_assets.dash: DASH — Dash, fast-confirmation Bitcoin-family chain (since 2014). Trade-only on {brand}. Use a Dash wallet (Dash Core, Dash Electrum, hardware wallets); accepts X… P2PKH and 7… P2SH addresses. Optional PrivateSend mixing via masternodes — pre-mix before sharing the address for stronger privacy.
section_assets.usdc: USD Coin stablecoin. Centralized — Circle can freeze any address. Trade-only.
section_assets.dai: DAI — MakerDAO USD-pegged stablecoin. Multi-network (ERC-20/Polygon/Base/Arbitrum, all EVM). Trade-only. Partly USDC-backed.
section_assets.doge: DOGE — Dogecoin, transparent proof-of-work chain (since 2013), merge-mined with Litecoin. Trade-only on {brand}. Use a Dogecoin wallet (Dogecoin Core, MyDoge, hardware wallets); accepts D… P2PKH and 9…/A… P2SH addresses. No native privacy upgrade —
section_assets.zec: ZEC — Zcash, proof-of-work chain with optional zero-knowledge shielded transactions (Sapling + Orchard pools). Supports both transparent (t1/t3, base58, similar to Bitcoin's legacy addresses) and shielded (zs1/u1, bech32, hides sender/recipient/amount) addresses. Trade-only — cannot pay listing fees.
section_assets.arrr: ARRR — Pirate Chain.  Proof-of-work cryptocurrency with chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool (every transaction is private by construction).  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use a Pirate Chain wallet (Treasure Chest, Pirate.Black, Verus); only one address format exists (zs1 Sapling shielded, 78 chars — visually identical to Zcash Sapling).
section_assets.dcr: Decred. A coin whose holders vote on how it's run. Public ledger like Bitcoin, with an optional privacy mode in its wallet.
section_assets.sol: SOL — Solana.  High-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use a Solana wallet (Phantom, Solflare, Cake Wallet for SOL, Trust Wallet); 32-44 character base58 addresses.  Send native SOL — not wrapped SOL or SPL tokens.  No native protocol-level mixing; wallet-side address rotation is the privacy lever.
section_assets.eth: ETH — Ethereum.  Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use an Ethereum wallet (MetaMask, Rabby, Frame, Rainbow, Trust Wallet); 42-character 0x-prefixed hex addresses.  Send native ETH — not wrapped ETH (WETH) or ERC-20 tokens.  No native protocol-level mixing; wallet-side address rotation is the privacy lever.  ENS names not resolved — paste raw 0x addresses.
section_assets.xrp: XRP — Ripple.  Federated Byzantine Agreement consensus on the XRP Ledger.  Trade-only on {brand}.  Use an XRPL wallet (Xaman/Xumm, Crossmark, Bifrost, GemWallet, Trust Wallet); 24-34-char base58 addresses starting with `r`.  Destination tags required when sending to exchange-hosted addresses (32-bit integer routing).  Accounts need ≥1 XRP base reserve to exist.  No native protocol-level mixing; wallet-side address rotation is the privacy lever.
section_assets.barter: Barter — goods or services, not a coin. Price your wares in local currency, pick the crypto(s) you'll accept (e.g. XMR, BTC, DOGE), and describe exactly what you're offering in the Terms. The listing needs no crypto address; you settle in whichever accepted crypto the buyer picks. Trade-only on {brand}.

section_recovery.heading: If something goes wrong
section_recovery.lost_seed_body: There is no recovery path. {brand} has no copy. If you still have access to the device, move funds out NOW and start a new account.
section_recovery.lost_password_body: Click "Sign in" and choose "Import seed phrase". Type your 12 words. Set a new password.
section_recovery.lost_device_body: On a new device, go to {brand} (or another Morphit site you trust), click "Sign in", choose "Import seed phrase", type your 12 words. Set a new password.
section_recovery.suspect_compromise_body: Move funds to a new account immediately. Anyone with the seed has full control. There's no "freeze" button on a blockchain.

compare.heading: Compare orderbooks
compare.lede: See if two Morphit instances are serving the same orderbook. Useful when you suspect an instance is hiding orders (censorship), or just want to confirm they agree.

input.label: Compare with another Morphit instance
input.hint: Paste the URL of a second Morphit instance (e.g. https://example.org).

results.heading: Comparison
results.interpretation: A small disparity is normal — the two instances may be at slightly different indexed blocks. A large or persistent disparity across refreshes is the real signal.

pane.in_both_note: Orders both instances agree on. Listed briefly — these are not the censorship signal.

url_error.invalid_scheme: URL must use http:// or https://.
url_error.bad_host: URL host is missing or too long.

error.same_instance: That's the same instance you are on. Pick a different one to compare against.
error.local_failed: Could not fetch that instance's orderbook: {reason}
error.remote_failed: Could not fetch {host}'s orderbook: {reason}. The remote instance may be offline, unreachable, or blocking this request.
error.fetch_threw: Couldn't reach {host}. Network error or the instance is offline.
error.local_timeout: The orderbook took too long to load. Try again in a moment.
error.unknown_instance: {host} is not a registered Morphit instance, so it can't be compared. Pick one from the instance list.
error.remote_unreachable: This instance could not reach {host}. It may be offline or unreachable from here right now; try again later.
error.remote_bad_answer: {host} answered, but not with a Morphit orderbook.
error.busy: Too many comparisons right now. Try again in a minute.

footer.snapshot_note: This is a one-shot snapshot; both sides may have changed in the seconds between fetches. Refresh a few times over a minute or two to see a persistent pattern.

verdict.agree_body: Across the orders both instances could be compared on, every one appears on both. {n} orders matched. Nothing is being hidden by {host} in the range checked.
verdict.differ_body: Some orders appear on only one of the two instances. Check the block gap first — if the instances are at different heights, the newest orders legitimately differ. A difference that survives several re-runs is the real signal.
verdict.inconclusive_body: Both instances returned a capped page of orders and the pages do not overlap, so there is no range in which both are known to be complete. Nothing can be concluded from this comparison.
verdict.malformed_heading: One instance sent an impossible answer
verdict.malformed_body: {host} says it has more orders but sent none of them. The first page of an orderbook that has orders always contains some, so this is how an instance hiding its orders would answer. Re-run in a few minutes; if it keeps answering this way, prefer another instance.

window.truncated_note: At least one instance had more orders than it could return in one page, so the comparison was limited to the range where both are known to be complete. {excluded} orders fell outside that range and could not be checked either way.

error.identity_mismatch: Couldn't sign — your account session looks out of sync. Sign out, then sign back in to fix this.

why_agpl.q: Why does Morphit use the AGPL-3.0 license?
why_agpl.a:
So that nobody — not a company, not a government, not even us — can take Morphit, lock it up, and quietly turn it against the people using it.

**The one rule it adds.** If you change Morphit and let people use your changed copy over the network, you must offer them its source code. Everything else is allowed: run your own instance, rebrand it, add features, charge for it. You just can't run a *secret, modified* version — which is how anyone can check that a site runs real Morphit and not a backdoored look-alike.

**Why not a looser license?** Permissive licenses (MIT, BSD, Apache) would let anyone close the code, add hidden tracking, and sell it back as a surveillance app. The plain GPL has a gap for websites: its sharing rule applies when you hand out the program, not when you run a changed copy on your own server — which is exactly how Morphit is used. The AGPL closes that gap. No license at all is worse: the law then reserves all rights, so nobody could legally fork it.

**For agorists.** Yes, copyright is a tool of the State. Copyleft turns it against enclosure: every fork stays open, every instance stays checkable. So fork Morphit, run an instance, and talk three friends into running more.

*Morphit is licensed under the GNU AGPL, version 3 or later. This is our reasoning, not legal advice.*

what_is_morphit.a:
{brand} is a peer-to-peer marketplace where people trade cash for cryptocurrency ({coins}) directly with each other. You can barter goods and services too.

{brand} never holds your cash or coins, and never asks who you are. Think of it as a public bulletin board for trades (a decentralised bulletin board service, or DBBS) — not a bank or an exchange.

is_it_safe.a:
Safer than sites that hold your funds, because {brand} can't lose, freeze or run off with funds it never has. The coins go straight from one trader to the other.

The real risk is the person you trade with, and nobody can reverse a trade that goes wrong. So before you trade, open their profile and check their reputation: completed trades, star rating, written feedback, and when they last traded. A green sprout 🌱 next to a name means "New trader": fewer than 4 completed trades.

An account name is all {brand} knows about who anyone is — @scooby or @dingleberry, it doesn't matter. Reputation is earned by trading honestly. With someone new, start with a small trade.

vs_others.q: How is {brand} different from LocalBitcoins or LocalMonero?
vs_others.a:
LocalBitcoins (closed 2023) and LocalMonero (closed 2024) were companies. They held your coins in escrow during a trade, and their staff settled disputes. When they shut down, their users' reputations and trade history went with them.

{brand} works differently:
• **No custody.** {brand} never holds your coins. The seller sends straight to the buyer.
• **No company to shut down.** Orders, feedback and encrypted chat live on the Blurt blockchain. Anyone can run an instance, and instances can be reached over the normal web, Tor, I2P and Lokinet.
• **Private chat.** Messages are end-to-end encrypted on your device. Operators can't read them.
• **Your account is yours.** Your keys stay in your browser, and your 12-word seed opens your account on any device or instance.

**The trade-off:** no escrow, no arbitrator, nobody to appeal to. Feedback is signed and permanent, so a scammer's record follows them forever — but nothing protects you from a first-time scammer. Check reputation and start small.

Morphit will never add escrow or arbitration: that would bring back the middleman it exists to remove.

vs_atomic_swap_dexes.a:
BasicSwap is a kindred no-middleman project to Morphit: it does atomic swaps (a coin-for-coin trade that either completes for both people or not at all) directly between two crypto wallets, with no escrow and no central server. We share the principle; the trade-offs differ.

• **Install vs. browser.** BasicSwap is a desktop app that usually runs a full node for each coin, which can take hours or days to sync. {brand} is a web page — nothing to install.
• **Both online vs. any time.** A swap needs both people online until it finishes, and the coins stay locked until it does. If the other side disappears, you wait for a refund timer. On {brand} you post an order and the other person answers whenever they're ready.
• **Crypto only vs. cash too.** BasicSwap trades coin for coin. {brand} also does cash, payment apps and barter.
• **Reputation and chat.** BasicSwap has neither. {brand} has signed on-chain feedback and encrypted chat.

On 14 July 2026, BasicSwap was exploited for more than 0.66 BTC (about $42,000), as confirmed by its own developer and by Orangefren. We mention it so you can choose with the facts, not to gloat: {brand} never holds your coins, so there is nothing to drain. Software can have bugs, but they are constantly being scanned for.

Both designs are valid. They suit different people.

vs_bisq_haveno.q: How is {brand} different from Bisq or Haveno/Retoswap?
vs_bisq_haveno.a:
Bisq and Haveno (and Haveno's fork RetoSwap) are the closest projects to ours in spirit: non-custodial, peer-to-peer, no KYC. Haveno is a fork of Bisq, so they work much the same way.

The main differences:
• **Desktop app vs. browser.** Bisq and Haveno are desktop apps. {brand} runs in any browser, phones included, with nothing to install.
• **Escrow vs. reputation.** On Bisq and Haveno, both traders lock coins plus a security deposit in a multisig escrow (2-of-3 on Haveno), and arbitrators settle disputes. {brand} has no escrow, no deposit and no arbitrator — you rely on the other trader's signed, on-chain reputation.
• **More to trade.** Every Haveno trade involves Monero. {brand} trades many coins, plus cash and barter.
• **More ways in.** {brand} instances can be reached over the clearnet/normal web, Tor, I2P, ENS and Lokinet.

An escrow-and-arbitrator safety net is also something to attack. Haveno's trade protocol was exploited on 20 May 2026 (about $2.7 million, using a forged arbitrator message) and again on 16 June 2026 through its dispute process (about 1,500 XMR, by early estimates). RetoSwap paused trading both times. Bisq has also been hacked in the past, with user funds stolen.

{brand} has no arbitrator, escrow or dispute payout for attacks like these to target. The price is that you alone decide who to trust. Reputation is everything.

vs_openmonero.a:
OpenMonero (a LocalMonero clone) is custodial: it keeps users' coins in its own wallet — and it has lost them. On 6 June 2025, a server misconfiguration let attackers drain about 77.85 XMR (about $25,225); OpenMonero says it has been repaying users out of its trading fees ever since. On 21 May 2026 it posted a new exploit alert and told users to stop all payments. It has since added server hardening, but that protects a wallet that is still there to lose.

{brand} keeps no wallet of users' coins. The seller sends XMR straight to the buyer, so there is nothing on a {brand} server to drain or freeze, and no operator who could vanish holding your coins.

We are fully open source with no hidden code: everything that runs in your browser is published and can be checked. OpenMonero obfuscates parts of its code, so you can't fully check what it does with your funds.

video_tutorial.a:
Yes. Short video tutorials are posted on [blurt.media](https://blurt.media), a video site on the Blurt network — search for "Morphit".

We link out instead of embedding: {brand} doesn't embed videos or other sites, and some video players share video peer-to-peer, which can show your internet connection to other viewers. If that worries you, watch through a VPN or Tor Browser.

signup_requirements.q: What do I need to sign up?
signup_requirements.a:
Nothing personal. No email, no phone number, no name, no ID.

• Your browser makes your account keys right on your device. They never leave it.
• Write down your 12-word seed on paper. It's your master key to get back into your account on a new device — nobody else can restore it.
• Pick a public account name (3–16 lowercase letters, digits or dashes, starting with a letter). It's free: {brand} pays the Blurt network cost.

That's it.

how_to_buy.a:
1. Open the orderbook and filter it by the coin you want.
2. Pick a seller with a good reputation, open their order and tap **Message**.
3. In the chat, agree on the amount, the price and how you'll pay — cash, a payment app, goods, whatever you both accept.
4. Tap **Share crypto address** to send the seller your wallet address.
5. Pay the seller as agreed. Once they have your payment, they send the crypto straight to your wallet.
6. Leave each other feedback. Done!

{brand} never holds anything in between, so choose sellers carefully and start small.

how_to_sell.a:
1. Tap Post, choose **I want to SELL**, and pick the coin — Monero, for example.
2. Set the value range and price, tick the payment methods you accept, and optionally add your location.
3. When a buyer messages you, agree on the details in the chat.
4. Once you've really received their payment, send the crypto to the address they share in the chat (the **Pay now** button sends or records it).
5. Leave honest feedback — it helps everyone.

Your very first order must be a buy of BLURT, and it's usually free (see "Is my first order really free?"); after that you can post sell orders. Posting costs a small listing fee — see "What are the fees?".

fees.a:
**{brand} never takes a cut of your trade.** The price you agree is the price you get, and {brand} never touches your funds.

**Posting an order costs a small listing fee:**
• About **$0.125** (in US-dollar value) if you pay in BLURT — half price.
• About **$0.25** if you pay in BTC or XMR, where this site accepts them.
The post screen shows the exact amount before you sign. BLURT is the default (Morphit runs on the Blurt blockchain), and BLURT-paid fees count toward loyalty rewards (see "How do loyalty rewards work? (The BP milestones I saw mentioned)").

**Your first order is free** — it's a buy of BLURT. See "Is my first order really free?".

**Lots of orders cost more (BLURT only).** Counting the orders you have live or posted in the last 24 hours, the first 3 cost the base fee. From the 4th, each costs 25% more than the one before, and 50% more after the 10th. This stops spammers; the post screen shows your tier. BTC and XMR fees stay flat.

**Optional extras:**
• A featured slot at the top of the orderbook: you bid BLURT per hour, for at least 6 hours.
• Messaging someone about one of their live orders is free, and so are all replies. A first message to anyone else costs 5 BLURT (more if you message many strangers within a few minutes).

Blurt itself also charges a tiny network fee on each transaction.

trade_goods_services.q: Can I trade goods or services on {brand}, like fruit trees or vintage records?
trade_goods_services.a:
**Yes — and for some people this is the whole point of {brand}.** If you're unbanked, living under capital controls, or watching your currency lose value, turning your goods and your work straight into hard money — without asking a bank's permission — is a lifeline. That's counter-economics in practice.

**Two ways to do it:**
• **Sell goods or services for crypto.** Tap Post, choose **I want to SELL**, and pick **BARTER** as the asset. Set its value in your local currency, tick the cryptos you'll accept, and describe your offer in **Terms**. One listing covers every coin you accept.
• **Pay for crypto with goods.** On a normal order — say, **I want to BUY** Monero — add **Barter (goods/services)** as a payment method and describe your offer in **Terms**.

*Example Terms:* "$20 per orange tree, 1–2 m tall. Pick up at my farm, or I'll ship for $5 more per tree." Or: "I'll come and wash your car for $30. Wax is $20 extra."

**The one rule:** one side of every trade is a coin that {brand} supports. That's what lets honest traders build a reputation that travels with them.

cash_by_mail_walkthrough.q: How do I trade cash by mail or ship physical goods through {brand}?
cash_by_mail_walkthrough.a:
It works like any other {brand} trade, plus two chat buttons. They show up when the chat is about a live order that accepts **Cash by mail**, **Barter (goods/services)** or **Precious metals**.

**Share mailing address** — for the person sending the crypto. Fill in country, street, city and postal code (name, apartment, state and a note are optional). Only the two of you can read it (end-to-end encrypted), but once sent, your partner has it for good — a P.O. box or mail-drop is safer than your home address.

**Record shipment** — for the person mailing the cash or goods. Pick the carrier (or Other), enter the tracking number from your receipt, and add a note if you like. Your partner sees a **Shipped via** card with a **Track package** link.

**Safety tips:**
• Use a tracked, insured service and a plain envelope or box.
• Mailing cash? Wrap it in aluminum foil, and use the postal service — UPS and FedEx forbid cash. Never lie on customs forms.
• Sellers: look up the tracking number on the carrier's site and check it's headed to *your* ZIP or postal code. A scammer can paste someone else's number.
• Send the crypto only after the package arrives and you've counted it.

**Limits:** {brand} can't settle disputes or reverse anything. Lost mail without insurance is simply lost. If someone takes your cash and never pays, leave honest feedback to warn others. Start with small trades.

order_timeouts.q: How long do orders stay open?
order_timeouts.a:
You choose when you post: 1, 3, 7, 14, 30, 60 or 90 days. The default is 90 days; a free first order runs for 7 days. When the time is up, the order expires and leaves the orderbook.

You can cancel an open order at any time, and you have 15 minutes after posting to fix mistakes (see 'Can I fix or cancel an order after posting?').

When an order has expired or you cancelled it, the **Re-list this order** button in [My orders](/my/orders) fills in a new order with the same details for you to check. A re-listed order is a new order, with a new listing fee.

How long the trade itself takes is up to you and your trade partner. {brand} sets no deadline; you agree on it in the chat.

order_editing.q: Can I fix or cancel an order after posting?
order_editing.a:
**Fixing:** for 15 minutes after posting, {brand} lets you edit an order from [My orders](/my/orders): amounts, price, payment methods, region and terms. Editing is free. You can't change buy or sell, the coin or the currency; for that, cancel and post a new order. After 15 minutes the order is locked.

**Cancelling:** you can cancel an open order at any time.

Why only 15 minutes? It is enough to catch a typo, but too short to lure buyers with one price and quietly change it later.

Nothing is erased: the blockchain keeps the original, every edit and the cancellation, so anyone can check an order's history.

chat_privacy.a:
What you write in {brand}'s encrypted chat is private. Messages are end-to-end encrypted: only you and your trade partner can read them. Not {brand}, not the operator, not anyone reading the blockchain.

What others **can** see, because chat is stored on the public Blurt chain:
• who and when (@scooby chatted with @alice yesterday)
• which order a chat is about
• roughly how long each message is
• when you read a conversation (read receipts)
• whom you block

There is no forward secrecy: anyone who later gets your keys can read your past messages. For very sensitive talk, use a dedicated messenger such as **Signal**, **Session** or **Matrix/Element**.

The tech: X25519 key agreement that mixes a fresh one-time key per message with both people's long-term keys (which proves who sent it), ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption and BLAKE2b, all from libsodium.

monero_amount_jitter.q: Why does {brand} randomize my transfer amount?
monero_amount_jitter.a:
So nobody can match your payment to your order.

If an order says 0.005 BTC and exactly 0.005 BTC appears on the blockchain, anyone watching can link the two. So when you share your receiving address in the chat, {brand} adds a tiny random extra ("jitter") to the amount the buyer should send. The seller always gets slightly **more**, never less.

Monero hides amounts on its chain, but the figure still travels through chats, screenshots, wallets and exchanges. The extra helps there too.

The extra is at most:
• XMR: 0.000000999999
• BTC, BCH, LTC, DASH, DOGE, ZEC, ARRR, DCR: 999 satoshis (0.00000999)
• ETH, XRP, USDT, USDC, DAI: 0.000999
• SOL: 0.000000999
• BLURT: 0.099

It is on by default; the switch is under the amount when you share your address. Turn it off only when you must send an exact figure, such as an invoice. It does not protect against USDT or USDC freezes; see the [privacy guides](/privacy) for each coin.

feedback_immutable.q: Can feedback be edited or deleted?
feedback_immutable.a:
No. Once posted, a review stays on the blockchain for good. Nobody can quietly change or erase it: not you, not the reviewer, not {brand}. That is what makes a reputation worth something.

If someone reviews you unfairly, you can post a public reply under it. The review stays, but everyone can read your side.

**If people are going to trust you, your reputation is everything.**

data_collection.q: What data does {brand} collect about me?
data_collection.a:
Very little, and nothing about who you are. No phone number, ID, cookies, analytics or tracking, and no email address unless you give one for Offline Notifications.

What does exist:
• **Your IP address.** It reaches the server as on any website. Morphit's code keeps it in memory only, for rate limits (at most 24 hours), and never writes it to disk.
• **What your browser asks for.** Orders, chats and the things you send go through this site's server, so its operator can see which accounts and orders you look at, and your signed actions before the blockchain does.
• **What you publish.** Orders, reviews and chat messages (encrypted, but with sender, recipient and time) are public on the Blurt chain.
• **Push notifications**, if you turn them on: the site keeps your account name with your browser's push address until you turn them off.
• **Offline Notifications**, if you turn them on: the site keeps the address you gave for them (email, Matrix, Session, XMPP or Telegram), encrypted, until you delete it.

lost_keys.q: What if I lose my password or recovery seed?
lost_keys.a:
Nobody can recover your account for you: not {brand}, not the operator. That is on purpose. A recovery button would mean someone else holds a copy of your keys.

• **Forgot your password?** Sign in again with your 12-word recovery phrase and pick a new password.
• **Lost your 12 words, but still signed in somewhere?** Open [Back up my keys](/backup-keys) now and write them down again.
• **Lost both?** The account is gone for good. You'll need a new one.

Signed in with an existing Blurt account? Then your backup is your Keyfile (with its password) or your Blurt keys. Lose them and no one can restore them.

what_is_blurt.q: Why did Morphit choose the Blurt blockchain?
what_is_blurt.a:
Morphit needs a public notice board that nobody owns. Orders, reviews and chats must be readable and checkable by anyone, without trusting one company's server. Blurt is a social blockchain built for exactly this kind of public, signed data.

Why Blurt fits:
• **Fast.** A new block about every 3 seconds, so new orders show up in seconds.
• **Cheap.** Each action costs a tiny BLURT fee, with no bidding wars over fees. (The listing fee is set by Morphit, not by the chain.)
• **Anonymous but accountable.** Accounts need no email, ID or real name, yet every review is signed and permanent, so nobody can forge or erase someone's record.
• **No central server.** Every Morphit site reads the same chain and shows the same orders. If one site closes, the orders are still there.
• **Room for private chat.** Morphit stores chats on Blurt as encrypted messages that only you and your trade partner can read.

Why not Monero? It hides data by design, which is great for money but wrong for a public orderbook. And on chains with busy fee markets, posting every order and message would cost far more.

privacy_mode.q: What is the most private way to sign in?
privacy_mode.a:
Sign in for this session only, a kind of privacy mode. Pick **Seed phrase every time (most private)** when you set up, or **keep me signed in just for this session** when you sign in with your 12 words.

Then nothing is saved on the device. Your keys stay only in memory, in this browser's open {brand} tabs, and are gone once you close them. Next time, you type your 12 words again. Use this on shared or public computers.

The other choice, **Password (fast)** or **Remember me**, saves your keys on this device, encrypted with a password you pick, so you can unlock quickly next time. They stay until you **Sign Out**.

In a session-only sign-in, your chat read marks and recent chat partners are kept in that tab only, too.

use_vpn.q: Can I use a VPN to access {brand}?
use_vpn.a:
Yes, and we recommend it. A VPN hides your real location from this site, and hides from your internet provider which sites you visit. Our favorite is Mullvad (mullvad.net), and they accept Monero too.

One tip: new accounts are limited each day per internet connection (2 by default), and many VPN users share one connection. If sign-up says the daily limit is reached, switch to another VPN server and try again.

activity_level.q: How much activity is there on {brand} right now?
activity_level.a:
See the [stats page](/stats). It shows active orders, total orders, trades (all time and the last 30 days), and how many coins and currencies have orders right now. A trade counts once it gets a review (once, even when both people review each other).

The numbers come from this site's indexer reading the public Blurt chain. Every order is a signed record on that chain, so anyone can recount them with their own indexer, without asking anyone's permission. The same numbers are available as JSON for dashboards.

sybil_protection.a:
In three ways:

• **A review needs a real conversation.** You can only review someone you have actually chatted with: at least 2 messages each way, over at least 15 minutes. Nobody can review themselves.
• **Orders cost money.** Each order has a small listing fee. Paid in BLURT, the fee climbs fast from your 4th order that is open or posted in the last 24 hours. Fake orders get expensive.
• **Suspicious patterns don't count.** The indexer looks for accounts that seem to be the same person, such as two accounts swapping 5-star reviews or a group of new accounts ganging up on someone. Their reviews are marked 'Not counted toward the rating', and a pair already caught swapping reviews can't post new ones.

no_js.a:
Only partly. With JavaScript off you can read pages with fixed text, like the security page, the glossary and the run-a-node page, and the list of FAQ questions. The FAQ answers, the privacy guides, the orderbook, profiles, reviews and chat are loaded by JavaScript, so without it they stay empty.

To follow orders without JavaScript, use the RSS feeds in any feed reader (see 'Can I follow {brand} with RSS?').

Trading needs JavaScript because all the cryptography (your keys, signing, chat encryption) happens inside your browser. Doing it on a server would mean the server holds your keys, and {brand} refuses to do that.

rss_feeds.a:
Yes. There are three feeds, each in three formats: RSS (`.xml`), Atom (`.atom`) and JSON Feed (`.json`). Click an orange RSS button on the site to copy a link, then paste it into any feed reader. No account needed.

• **All orders:** `/rss/orderbook.xml`, the 50 newest live orders. The button is in the footer.
• **One coin:** `/rss/orderbook/by-asset/btc.xml` (or `xmr`, and so on). Pick a coin on the orderbook; the button sits next to **Clear filters**.
• **One trader:** `/rss/orderbook/by-account/@alice.xml`. The button is on their profile, below their orders.

If you set filters on the orderbook (buy or sell, currency, payment method…), the feed link includes them.

Privacy: the feeds show nothing that isn't already public on the chain. But someone watching your connection may see which feed you check. A trader's feed shows you follow that trader, and a filtered link shows what you are looking for. Use Tor if that matters to you.

why_fresh_addresses.q: Why should I use a new receiving address each time?
why_fresh_addresses.a:
So your trades can't be linked together.

On public chains like Bitcoin, anyone can look up an address. If you use the same one for every trade, a stranger can add up all your trades: how many, when, and how much. Monero hides addresses on its chain, but everyone you give the same address to can tell the payments go to the same person.

A new address for each trade breaks that link. Your wallet makes new addresses for free, usually in a click or two.

• **Monero:** use a new subaddress (it starts with 8) for each trade. {brand} also accepts a main address (starts with 4), but shows a tip suggesting a subaddress.
• **Every coin:** {brand} won't block a reused address, but if you shared it from this device before, you'll see a warning. That check stays on your device.

who_runs_it.a:
Morphit is the open source software that runs this site and anyone can run a copy of it. The morphit.io site for example, is run by Agorise, the Dev Team of the software.

The design assumes that any one site may go offline which is why this site is syndicated, push-mirrored and federated across multiple networks like Tor and I2P. Orders, reviews and encrypted chats live on the Blurt chain, so other sites (on the clearnet (normal web), Tor, I2P, ENS or Lokinet) read the same data, and your keys work on any of them.

run_your_own.q: Can I run my own Morphit?
run_your_own.a:
Yes, and please do. Morphit only stays unstoppable if many people run it. One install gives you everything:

• **The website:** at your own domain, at a .onion or .b32.i2p address, or all of them.
• **An indexer:** reads the Blurt chain, serves orders, chats and profiles to your visitors (also as an API and RSS feeds), and talks to the other Morphit sites.
• **A relay:** creates Blurt accounts for your new users and sends push notifications. Your relay pays about 102 BLURT for each new account.

You need an Ubuntu 24.04 server: a cheap VPS or an old PC with 2 CPUs, 4 GB of RAM and 80 GB of disk. One command installs it, and a wizard asks a few questions; docs/RUN-A-MORPHIT-NODE.md walks you through it. You earn 90% of the BLURT listing fees paid on your site.

**Going fully hidden:** a node can run with no clearnet at all. Everything goes over Tor and I2P, and a firewall rule blocks the rest. The directory then shows "Zero use of clearnet internet", which is the node's own claim that others cannot check. Start a hidden node with fresh keys and a fresh operator account, so it can't be linked to an old clearnet site.

security_attack_vectors.q: Is {brand} vulnerable to hacking, data theft, or takedowns?
security_attack_vectors.a:
The design leaves little to attack.

• **No key database.** Your keys are made in your browser and never sent to a server.
• **No logins to steal.** There are no server-side accounts, passwords or sessions to phish or hijack.
• **No personal data.** No KYC, and IP addresses are kept in memory only, for rate limits.
• **Nothing central to take down.** Orders live on the blockchain. If one site closes, every other site or indexer still shows them.

**For the technically minded:** inputs are checked and size-limited; database queries are parameterised; the Content-Security-Policy lets scripts load only from the site itself (no inline scripts, no eval; only WebAssembly, for the cryptography); other websites can read public data only, never with credentials, and every write must be JSON; the relay checks which site a signup came from, and sends push notifications only to allowed push services (the browser makers', plus any the operator adds). No PHP, no WordPress, no OAuth. Floods meet per-client rate limits and size caps; a huge DDoS is for the hosting provider to absorb.

One honest limit: the operator serves the page code, so a hostile operator can get around these defences. Pick operators you trust. The full threat model is in docs/SECURITY.md and docs/audit/.

security_engineering_rigor.q: How rigorous is Morphit's security review process?
security_engineering_rigor.a:
Security here leaves a public paper trail.

• **Published threat model.** `docs/audit/` holds the current STRIDE matrix, attack tree and red-team narrative. Each threat says what the code does, whether a named test proves it, and what is still open and why.
• **Open source.** Morphit is AGPL-3.0, at git.agorise.net/agorise/morphit. Anyone can read it, run its tests and send fixes. We assume the attacker has read every line.
• **Little to leak.** No KYC, email, phone or session cookies. Keys are made and encrypted in your browser, and chat is end-to-end encrypted. IP addresses stay in memory only, for rate limits. What is public on chain is listed in `docs/METADATA-LEAK-CATALOG.md`.
• **Monero.** Morphit never holds your XMR, never asks for a view key and never sends your transactions. A transaction key is published only when you pay a listing fee in XMR, so anyone can check that payment.
• **No security by secrecy.** Rate limits, fees and what it costs to make fake accounts are all written down (`docs/OPERATIONS.md`, `docs/FEES-AND-REWARDS.md`).

**Found a vulnerability?** Send a private Matrix message to **@agorise:matrix.org**. Never post details in a public issue, a chat room or on chain. An engineer answers every actionable report, and findings that materially improve security are rewarded in BLURT or BTC, scaled to severity. Details: the [security page](/security#bounty) and `docs/SECURITY.md`.

help_make_unstoppable.q: How can I help make Morphit unstoppable?
help_make_unstoppable.a:
Every independent site makes Morphit harder to stop. Ways to help:

• **Run your own site.** See 'Can I run my own Morphit?'. Blocking one site does little when many others exist.
• **Add a hidden address.** A .onion, .b32.i2p or .loki address lets people reach Morphit where the normal web is blocked. These need no certificate and no domain name.
• **Point an ENS .eth name at your site**, usually through a copy on IPFS, so people can reach it at a decentralized name like `yourbrand.eth`. It shows up as an extra button in the footer.
• **Fund a site.** Send BLURT to an operator's relay account. Each new account costs the relay about 102 BLURT, so 500 sign-ups a week need about 51,000 BLURT.
• **Spread the word.** Tell your communities, write a blog post, make a tutorial.
• **Translate or improve the docs.** The code is open (AGPL-3.0): send a pull request at git.agorise.net/agorise/morphit.

There is no central company to pressure. Everyone who runs a piece of Morphit makes that stronger.

why_self_trading_fails.q: Why doesn't trading with myself work to boost my reputation?
why_self_trading_fails.a:
Because it costs real money and hardly helps your reputation.

• **Every listing costs a fee:** about $0.125 in BLURT or $0.25 in BTC/XMR. It goes to the site and the Morphit project, not to your other account. A trade only adds to your trade count when its listing was paid for. (Your one free first buy counts too, but only for you.)
• **Lots of orders cost more.** If you post many orders in a day (or keep many open), each BLURT-paid listing after the 3rd costs more: the 4th costs 1.25×, the 10th about 4.8×.
• **One partner counts once.** However many times the same account reviews you, only its latest review counts toward your score.
• **Fake pairs get spotted.** {brand} looks for accounts that seem to be one person: made by the same creator and first used minutes apart, swapping 5-star reviews only with each other, or aiming most of their reviews or trades at one account. Reviews and trades between flagged accounts don't count, and a warning can show on the profile.

Honest trading is cheaper, and it actually works.

why_multi_accounts_fail.q: Can I register many accounts through {brand} to spam the orderbook?
why_multi_accounts_fail.a:
You could try, but it's slow, it costs you, and it's easy to spot.

• **Signups are limited.** Each new account costs the site about 102 BLURT (Blurt's 100 BLURT account fee plus 2 BLURT to get started). So by default {brand} allows 2 signups per internet address per day, at least an hour apart, and the operator sets a daily cap for the whole site. Making accounts on Blurt yourself costs you the same account fee.
• **Orders cost money.** Each account gets just one free first buy. After that every listing costs about $0.125 in BLURT or $0.25 in BTC/XMR, and BLURT-paid fees climb after the 3rd order in a day.
• **The welcome bonus can't be grabbed at signup.** Each account gets it once, and only after paying for a listing and being reviewed on it by a chat partner.
• **Linked accounts get flagged.** Reviews and trades between accounts that look like the same person don't count toward reputation.

We publish these rules openly. Being a real trader is always the easier path.

blurt_benefits.q: What is Blurt and why does {brand} sometimes mention it?
blurt_benefits.a:
Blurt is the public blockchain {brand} runs on. Your account, orders, reviews and encrypted chat messages are all stored there. Its coin is BLURT.

Why it comes up:

• **Tiny network fees.** Blurt charges a very small BLURT fee for each action (an order, a review, an encrypted chat message), so keep a little liquid BLURT on hand. New accounts get 2 BLURT to start. See 'What is Mana on Blurt?'.
• **Cheaper listing fees.** Paying a listing fee in BLURT costs about $0.125, half the BTC/XMR price, and it's checked on chain right away. Where the site offers it, you can pay in BTC or XMR instead.
• **Rewards.** The welcome bonus and loyalty rewards come in BLURT and Blurt Power (BP).
• **Blurt Power.** BP earns you a nice % APR and gives your votes weight on Blurt social sites like blurt.media and blurt.blog.

You can trade {coins:-blurt|or} on {brand} without ever trading BLURT itself. You only need that little bit for network fees.

how_to_stake_blurt.q: How do I stake my Blurt (power up to BP) to earn interest?
how_to_stake_blurt.a:
Staking BLURT means turning it into **Blurt Power (BP)**. Blurt calls this "powering up." BP earns a small yearly reward (your wallet shows the current rate as "Earning … APR"), gives your votes more weight, and can earn curation rewards. It stays your own coin the whole time: not a deposit, not a loan.

**How:** open your [wallet](/my/wallet), choose **Power up**, enter how much BLURT, and confirm. Your own keys sign it on the Blurt chain; {brand} never holds your coins.

**Getting it back:** choose **Power down**. Blurt pays it back in weekly parts over 4 weeks. That's a Blurt rule, not a {brand} one.

where_does_blurt_price_come_from.q: Where does the Blurt price displayed on {brand} come from?
where_does_blurt_price_come_from.a:
{brand} uses the BLURT price for two things: showing a rough dollar value next to BLURT amounts, and working out how many BLURT a listing fee should be so it stays about 12.5¢.

Where it comes from, in order:

• **api.blurt.blog**, the Blurt community's own price service, whenever its answer looks sensible.
• If that's down or looks wrong: an average of several public price sites (CoinGecko, CoinPaprika, CryptoCompare, and others if the operator adds them), leaving out any that disagree too much.
• Optionally, a price worked out from trades on {brand} itself. It's off unless the operator turns it on, and it's only used when the sources above fail.
• With no recent price at all, the site asks for the standard BLURT fee amount and shows no dollar figure.

A site reached only over Tor and I2P never contacts these price sites; it asks other Morphit sites instead.

A bad price can't change what the network accepts: every site checks fees against a minimum set on the Blurt chain, not against its own price.

BTC and XMR prices come first from five Haveno and Bisq price servers reached over Tor. Their price is used only when at least two of them agree and they are most of the answers. If they don't agree, the site falls back to the public price sites (or, for a Tor/I2P-only site, to other Morphit sites).

The operator can show prices in a currency other than USD, such as EUR. Then the api.blurt.blog step is skipped, because it only quotes dollars.

where_to_buy_blurt.q: Where do I buy Blurt to use as a network fee?
where_to_buy_blurt.a:
**Right here on {brand}.** BLURT is one of the {coin_count} assets traded here, alongside {coins:-blurt}. Open the [orderbook](/orderbook), find someone selling BLURT, and message them. You pay them the way they accept (cash, bank transfer, another coin…), and they send BLURT to your account. No exchange account, no card, no KYC. You can also post your own buy order and let sellers come to you.

**Your first order can be free.** If your very first order is a buy of BLURT worth at least $1, {brand} covers the listing fee. See "Is my first order really free?"

**Once you have BLURT,** choose **Pay in BLURT** when you post an order, and the fee is sent from your BLURT balance when you sign.

first_order_free.q: Is my first order really free?
first_order_free.a:
Yes. If your very first order is a **buy of BLURT** worth at least **$1**, {brand} pays the listing fee for you. You enter the amount in your own currency, and the app checks it's worth at least $1.

**The rules:**
• It must be your very first order. Post any other order first and the free one is gone.
• It must be a buy of BLURT. You can pay the seller with cash, another coin, or whatever you agree on.
• One per account.

On the [post page](/post), the free option is already picked for your first order. If you switch to paying and post, the free order is gone.

**Why BLURT?** About $1 of BLURT covers roughly 8 future listing fees at the BLURT rate (about 12.5¢ each, half the BTC/XMR price), and paying fees in BLURT earns the welcome stake and loyalty rewards.

**What "free" means:** no listing fee for this one order. Blurt's tiny network fee still applies (new accounts get 2 BLURT for it). You and the seller trade directly; {brand} never touches your money.

**Reviews:** a review can't point to this free order (reviews need an order with a paid listing fee), so it can't earn you stars. Once you mark it completed, it still counts as one trade on your profile.

welcome_bonus.q: What is the welcome bonus and how do I earn it?
welcome_bonus.a:
There are two welcome rewards, then loyalty rewards:

**1. First BLURT-paid listing fee → a 1 BP welcome stake.** The site you posted through lends you 1 Blurt Power (BP), even if nobody trades with you. Blurt only lends BP in amounts of about 33 BP or more, so small rewards wait until they add up: for most traders, at the 500 BLURT loyalty milestone (61 BP in all).

**2. First completed trade on a listing you paid for → 10 BLURT, plus 10 BLURT powered up.** Once someone trades with you and reviews you on that listing, the site you posted through sends you 10 BLURT to spend and 10 BLURT as Blurt Power, both yours to keep. The free first buy doesn't count (it has no fee). Until 1 November 2026, if your first review comes from a trade on someone else's listing, this bonus is used up without being paid; from then on, that no longer happens.

**3. Loyalty rewards → up to 1,260 BP more.** See "How do loyalty rewards work? (The BP milestones I saw mentioned)".

Each reward comes once per account, from the relay of the site the order went through. Lent BP stays the site's. Waiting for a paid listing and a review stops fake accounts from farming bonuses.

loyalty_milestones.q: How do loyalty rewards work? (The BP milestones I saw mentioned)
loyalty_milestones.a:
Every listing fee you pay in BLURT adds to your lifetime total (on all Morphit sites). When it crosses a milestone, the site whose order crossed it lends you Blurt Power (BP):

• 100 BLURT paid → 10 BP
• 500 BLURT paid → 50 BP
• 2,000 BLURT paid → 200 BP
• 10,000 BLURT paid → 1,000 BP

**Good to know:**
• Only listing fees paid in BLURT count. BTC/XMR fees and the free first buy don't.
• Your total never resets or expires.
• Each milestone pays once, and they add up: crossing 100 and then 500 gives you 60 BP.
• It's a loan (a delegation), not a gift. The BP stays the site's, and its operator can take it back.
• Blurt only lends BP in amounts of about 33 BP or more, so small rewards wait until they add up: for most traders, at the 500 BLURT milestone (61 BP with the 1 BP welcome stake).

BP gives your votes weight on Blurt social sites like blurt.media and blurt.blog. With the 1 BP welcome stake, that's up to 1,261 BP lent to you. See also "What is the welcome bonus and how do I earn it?"

no_escrow_arbitration.q: Why no Escrow or Arbitration service?
no_escrow_arbitration.a:
Escrow is a babysitter who holds your money until the trade is done. An arbitrator is a referee who decides who's right when you argue.

The catch: you didn't want to trust a stranger, so now you have to trust the babysitter and the referee instead. They become a new middleman with power over your money. If they're dishonest, slow, biased or hacked, your money can still disappear.

So escrow and arbitration don't solve the trust problem; they just move it to someone else. {brand} never holds your money. Instead, you get public reviews to help you choose who to trade with, and a permanent, encrypted chat record of what you agreed.

Don't trust. Verify.

no_js_limits.q: What does the 'No JS' link in the footer do?
no_js_limits.a:
It links to this answer about how {brand} works without JavaScript. It isn't a switch: a website can't turn JavaScript off for you, only your browser can.

What still works with JavaScript off:
• Pages with fixed text, like the security page, the glossary and the run-a-node page. They are built ahead of time, so they still show. The FAQ shows its questions; its answers need JavaScript.
• The orderbook RSS feeds (`/rss/orderbook.xml`). They work in any feed reader.

What needs JavaScript:
• Live data: the orders in the orderbook, profiles, feedback and chat all load in your browser. So do the FAQ answers and the privacy guides.
• Anything you sign: posting orders, chatting, leaving feedback. Your keys and the cryptography stay inside your browser, never on a server, and that takes JavaScript.

how_to_run_node.q: How do I run a Morphit node?
how_to_run_node.a:
A Morphit node is your own copy of the marketplace, on a computer you control. It runs three parts: the website, the indexer (reads the Blurt blockchain and serves orders and chat) and the relay (creates new users' accounts and pays their rewards). You don't run a blockchain node: the indexer reads public Blurt nodes.

What you need:
• A computer that stays on, rented (a VPS) or an old PC, with 2+ CPUs, 4+ GB RAM and 80+ GB of drive space, running Ubuntu 24.04 or a 24.04-based system like Linux Mint 22. See "What are the minimum hardware requirements to run a Morphit node?"
• A web address, or none if you run Tor-only.
• A Blurt account holding BLURT to pay for your users' signups.
