To install, download the release, run `sudo bash morphit-setup.sh`, choose "Full guided install" and answer the wizard's questions. Then run `sudo morphit-ops register` to register as an operator. The walkthrough is at [/run-a-node](/run-a-node); the full reference is `docs/OPERATIONS.md`.

Why do it? You earn 90% of the BLURT listing fees paid on your site (see "How do operators earn?"), and your community gets one more door into the same marketplace if another site is blocked.

customize_your_instance.q: Can I customize the look of my own Morphit instance (logo, colours, name)?
customize_your_instance.a:
Yes. Your logo, icons, site name and colours can all be changed **without rebuilding**, so your site keeps serving the signed release and visitors never see the build-integrity warning. Copy your SVG files to the server, then run:

`sudo morphit-ops branding apply --logo /home/you/logo.svg --icon /home/you/icon.svg --name "Your Site"`

• `--logo`: the header and homepage logo. Add `--logo-footer` for a different footer logo.
• `--icon`: the browser-tab icon and the home-screen app icon.
• `--name`: your site's name. It replaces "Morphit" wherever the site names itself; mentions of the Morphit software and federation stay.
• Colours: add `--theme-from '#…' --theme-to '#…'`, or a preset such as `--theme champagne-gold`.

Prefer to be asked one question at a time? Run `sudo morphit-ops branding setup` (also *Branding* in the `sudo morphit-ops` menu). Every upgrade re-applies your branding. The full guide is `docs/BRANDING.md`.

Changing more, like fonts, layout or wording, means forking the code (it's built with SvelteKit). A rebuilt site no longer matches the signed release, so visitors' browsers show the build-integrity warning, by design, and you keep your fork up to date yourself.

One rule from the AGPL licence: if you run a **modified** version publicly, you must offer your changed source to your users. A footer link to your fork is enough.

how_operators_earn.a:
Most orders pay a small listing fee: about $0.125 in BLURT (half price, on purpose) or about $0.25 in BTC or XMR. Orders posted through your site carry your operator tag.

**BLURT fees: 90% to you, 10% to the Morphit treasury.** The user's own transaction pays both parts at once: 90% straight to your fees account, 10% to the treasury, which funds the project. Nobody holds your share, and nobody can withhold it.

**BTC and XMR fees: 100% to the Morphit treasury.** The Blurt chain can't split them, and splitting them by hand would mean someone holding your money.

**Also yours:** 90% of the featured-slot bids on your site (you set the hourly price; 50 BLURT/hour by default) and of the fees strangers pay to send a first message (from 5 BLURT).

**What you pay:** about 102 BLURT for every new account your relay creates (the chain's 100 BLURT fee plus 2 BLURT of starter funds); 10 BLURT plus 10 BLURT powered up when a user completes a first trade on a listing they paid for on your site; and 1 BLURT top-ups for active users who run low. Blurt Power rewards (a 1 BP welcome stake, loyalty rewards up to 1,260 BP per user) are lent, so that BLURT stays yours. Plus your server.

At a BLURT price of $0.002, your share of one listing is about 56 BLURT, so about two paid listings cover one new account.

how_to_find_good_operator.q: How do I find a good operator to use?
how_to_find_good_operator.a:
The [/operators](/operators) page lists every registered operator: their tag, when they registered, a contact link, how many orders came through their site and what they have earned.

Good signs:
• **A long track record.** Registered long ago and still active.
• **Real use.** Many orders came through their site, so real traders trust it.
• **A reachable person.** Their contact link leads to someone with a reputation outside {brand}.

What matters less is looks or language. Every Morphit site reads the same blockchain, so they show the same orders, unless an operator chooses to hide some. [/compare](/compare) checks whether another site shows the same orderbook as this one.

Why the choice still matters: no operator holds your money, because your keys stay in your browser. But the operator gets 90% of the BLURT listing fees you pay there, and serves the page code your browser runs. A dishonest one could show you false data, or ship code that copies your keys when you unlock them. The in-page release check catches a changed file on an honest operator's server, not an operator who serves the checker too.

So pick an operator with a long public track record, compare sites when something matters, or run your own.

what_is_morphit_chat.a:
{brand} chat is private messaging between two traders. Each message is locked (encrypted) on your device, stored on the Blurt blockchain, and unlocked only on the other person's device. Operators pass messages along but can't read them.

• **No setup.** Your chat key is made from your account's posting key the first time you open chat.
• **It lasts.** Close the tab and come back tomorrow: the conversation is still there, because it lives on the blockchain, not on one company's server.
• **Check once.** Compare the safety number with each partner once (⋮ → Verify peer) to make sure nobody swapped a key.

What is *not* private. Anyone reading the chain can see:
• who and when (@scooby chatted with @alice yesterday)
• roughly how long each message is
• which order a conversation is about, how far you have read, and whom you block

One more limit: your operator serves the app itself, so you are trusting their copy of the code. Pick operators you trust, or run your own. For sensitive details, use a metadata-private messenger such as Session (getsession.org) or Signal alongside {brand}.

chat_message_not_showing.q: My chat message or new conversation isn't showing up — is it lost or broken?
chat_message_not_showing.a:
Almost certainly not lost. {brand} chat is stored on the blockchain, and a brand-new conversation can take a moment to appear, sometimes on one side before the other, especially when you two use different Morphit sites.

• Your message goes out the moment you send it. The other person usually sees it within seconds.
• A conversation you just started can take up to about a minute to show in your inbox while your site catches up. Refreshing the page helps.
• Once a conversation exists, new messages in it arrive quickly.

Still missing after a few minutes? Tell your site's operator: their site may be behind on reading the blockchain.

chat_key_loss.q: What happens if I lose my chat key?
chat_key_loss.a:
You can't lose it on its own. Your chat key is made from your posting key (see 'Do I need to set up a separate key to use chat?'), so you only lose it if you lose access to your whole account.

Without your keys you can't post orders, leave feedback, send chat or read past messages, and {brand} can't recover them, because it never holds your keys.

Your safety net is the 12-word recovery phrase you wrote down at sign-up. Sign in with it and everything comes back, including past chats. (If you signed in with an existing Blurt account, your Keyfile and keys play that role.)

See 'What if I lose my password or recovery seed?' and 'How do I back up my {brand} account? What should I write down?'

why_chat_on_chain.q: Why is chat on the blockchain instead of a regular server?
why_chat_on_chain.a:
So chat doesn't depend on any one company's server.

• **No single off switch.** Every Morphit site reads the same blockchain. If one site goes down or is blocked, your conversations still exist and other sites can show them.
• **No silent edits.** Once a message is on the chain, nobody can change or delete it.
• **One source of truth.** There are no separate copies to keep in sync between sites.

The trade-offs:
• The content of each message is end-to-end encrypted, but who talks to whom and when (@bob with @sally yesterday), is public on the chain (see 'Are my chats private?').
• Messages usually arrive within a few seconds rather than instantly. That's fine for arranging a trade.

kyc_requirement.q: Does {brand} require KYC, identity verification, or government ID?
kyc_requirement.a:
No. {brand} is KYC-free: you never need to verify your identity. It never asks for your name, email, phone number, government ID, a selfie or proof of address. You pick an account name, and that's it.

{brand} never holds your money, so it has no reason to know who you are. Like any website, it does see your internet address while you're connected; use a VPN or Tor if you want to hide that.

If a site calling itself {brand} asks you for ID, it isn't {brand}. It's a scam. Close the tab.

how_to_trade_walkthrough.q: How do I trade on {brand} — a step-by-step walkthrough?
how_to_trade_walkthrough.a:
New here? Here's a first-time user's walkthrough, from start to finish.

1. **Create a free account.** Pick a name and a password. No email, no ID.
2. **Write down your 12-word recovery phrase** on paper and keep it safe. It's the only way back into your account.
3. **Find an offer** in the orderbook: the right coin, a fair price, a payment method you can use, and good feedback. Or post your own order.
4. **Message them** with the chat button on their order. Chat is encrypted.
5. **Agree on the details:** the exact amount, where to meet for cash or which account to pay, and who goes first.
6. **Trade.** One of you sends first; the other checks it arrived, then sends their side.
7. **Leave feedback** for each other, so future traders know whom to trust.

{brand} is the bulletin board that connects you. The trade itself happens directly between the two of you.

supported_countries.a:
Yes. The software has no country checks and no country blocks; it doesn't turn anyone away because of where they are. Orders live on a public blockchain, so you can browse, post and trade from anywhere with an internet connection.

If your country blocks this site, try its Tor, I2P, Lokinet or `.eth` addresses (the footer shows the ones this site has), or another Morphit site.

{brand} doesn't enforce any government's rules. Knowing your local laws, and deciding what to do about them, is up to you. #agorism #countereconomics

supported_fiat_currencies.q: Which fiat currencies (USD, EUR, local money) does {brand} support?
supported_fiat_currencies.a:
Practically all of them. When you post an order, you pick your currency from a list of about 150 circulating world currencies: USD, EUR, GBP, MXN, BRL, INR, NGN, ARS, PHP and many more. Search by name or code.

{brand} doesn't limit which one you use, and others filter the orderbook by the currencies they want, so they can find your offer.

counterparty_disappears.q: What happens if my trading partner disappears or stops responding mid-trade?
counterparty_disappears.a:
{brand} has no escrow, no referee and no customer service that can reverse a trade. If you send first and the other person vanishes, that money is gone. So protect yourself before you send:

• Trade with accounts that have a solid feedback history.
• For bigger amounts, split the trade into smaller pieces.
• Agree on every step in {brand}'s encrypted chat, so you both have a record.
• If you're selling, wait until the payment has fully cleared. Some bank payments can be reversed days later.

If someone cheats you, leave honest, detailed feedback with the facts, so the next person is warned. You get one review per trade, and it's permanent.

taxes.q: Do I owe taxes on trades I make through {brand}?
taxes.a:
That's between you and your tax authority. Most governments say yes, and their rules vary widely. We consider income tax theft; what you do is your choice.

{brand} doesn't report anything to anyone, and it doesn't know who you are. What it does give you is a permanent, public record of your orders and feedback on the blockchain, which you can look up any time if you need it.

Knowledge is power. #donoharm #agorism

mobile_desktop.q: Does {brand} work on mobile phones, iPad, or only desktop?
mobile_desktop.a:
Both. {brand} runs in any modern browser on a phone, tablet, laptop or desktop, and the layout fits small screens.

You can also add it to your home screen so it opens like an app: on iPhone or iPad use Safari, on Android use the browser menu. See 'Can I use {brand} on my iPhone or iPad?' and 'How do I install {brand} on Android?'. There's no app-store app and nothing to sideload.

Privacy setups work too, like GrapheneOS or Tor Browser. Tor Browser's "Safest" level turns JavaScript off, though, and {brand} can't run there.

privacy_practices.q: How do I trade anonymously or privately on {brand}?
privacy_practices.a:
{brand} already skips the big privacy leaks: no KYC, no email, no phone number. To go further:

• Use a VPN or Tor, so sites and nodes don't see your real IP address.
• Make a fresh account just for trading, separate from any you use for blogging.
• Never put your legal name or phone number in chat or order notes.
• Use a new receiving address for every trade (for Monero, a new subaddress from your wallet).
• Prefer Monero when you can. Its on-chain privacy is far stronger than Bitcoin's.
• For cash in person, meet in a neutral public place and share only what the meetup needs.

Remember that chats and orders leave public traces on the blockchain, such as who talked to whom (@bartsimpson with @dumbass), and when. Privacy is a habit, not a setting. For coin-by-coin advice, see the [privacy guides](/privacy) (for example [Bitcoin](/privacy/btc) or [Litecoin](/privacy/ltc)).

in_person_vs_online.q: Should I trade in person (cash meetup) or online (bank transfer)?
in_person_vs_online.a:
Both work. Pick what fits the trade size and how much you trust the other person.

• **Cash in person** is the most private: no bank, no paper trail. Meet in a busy public place in daylight, and bring a friend for bigger amounts. Don't part until the crypto has arrived.
• **Bank transfer or payment app** is convenient, but your bank sees it, and some payments can be reversed (chargebacks, recalled transfers). If you're selling, wait until the money has fully cleared. "Pending" isn't paid.

{brand} doesn't push either style.

scam_patterns.q: What scams should I watch out for on {brand}?
scam_patterns.a:
The common ones:

• **Reversible payments.** Someone pays with something they can undo after you've sent crypto, like a card chargeback or a recalled bank transfer. Only accept payments that truly clear first.
• **Moving you off {brand} chat.** A "trading partner" contacts you on WhatsApp or Telegram. {brand} chat is the only channel tied to their {brand} account, so stay there.
• **Fake sites.** Check the address bar, and bookmark the real site.
• **Too-good prices from new accounts.** No feedback and a price far better than the market is bait.
• **Small trades, then a big scam.** A few easy trades to win your trust, then one large trade that never pays.
• **Asking for your keys.** Nobody honest ever needs your 12 words or keys. {brand} warns you if you try to send something that looks like one.

Your best defence is feedback. Read it before every trade.

node_technical_skills.q: Do I need technical skills to run a Morphit node? How hard is it?
node_technical_skills.a:
Basic computer comfort is enough: opening a terminal, typing a command, and logging into a server over SSH if you rent one. If you've ever set up a home NAS, a VPN or a self-hosted app, you're ready.

Installing is one command, `sudo bash morphit-setup.sh`, followed by a wizard that asks plain-language questions. No file editing. It sets up the website, the database, HTTPS, the firewall and a Tor address for you. You need Ubuntu 24.04, or a 24.04-based system like Linux Mint 22.

No blockchain experience is needed. Morphit reads public Blurt nodes, so it's much closer to running a web app than running a blockchain node.

The step-by-step guide is at [/run-a-node](/run-a-node). You can ask for help in the public Matrix room `#agorise:matrix.org`.

node_hosting_costs.q: How much does it cost to host a Morphit node?
node_hosting_costs.a:
The server is cheap. The bigger cost is paying for your users' signups.

**The server.** You need 2+ CPUs, 4+ GB RAM and 80+ GB of drive space (SSD is best). Many hosting companies rent servers like that for a few dollars a month. Or use an old PC at home and pay only for the electricity.

**BLURT.** Your relay pays about 102 BLURT for each new account your site creates (the chain's 100 BLURT fee plus 2 BLURT of starter funds), so about 2,100 BLURT covers your first 20 signups. It also pays welcome bonuses and small top-ups. In return you get 90% of the BLURT fees paid on your site: listing fees, first-message fees and featured-slot bids (see "How do operators earn?").

A domain name is optional (about US$10 a year), or run Tor-only without one.

switching_instances.q: If one Morphit instance goes down, do I lose my orders and reputation?
switching_instances.a:
No. Your orders, profile, feedback and chats are stored on the Blurt blockchain, not on any one site. If one Morphit site goes down, any other one shows the same orders and the same reputation, read from the same chain. Nothing has to be moved.

You do have to sign in once on the new site. Your browser keeps your saved, encrypted keys separately for each website, so there you sign in with your 12-word seed phrase, your keyfile or your key.

An operator can hide listings on their own site, but never on anyone else's. Sites come and go; your reputation stays yours.

backup_practices.q: How do I back up my {brand} account? What should I write down?
backup_practices.a:
Write your 12-word recovery phrase on paper, in order, exactly as shown. Those 12 words rebuild every key {brand} uses, so they *are* your account.

• Keep the paper somewhere safe and offline, away from your computer — a fireproof box or a safe deposit box.
• For extra safety, make two copies and keep them in different places. For large amounts, stamp the words into a steel plate: metal survives fire and water, paper doesn't.
• Never photograph it, email it, or save it in a password manager that syncs to the cloud. An offline password manager such as KeePass is fine.
• Only ever type it into {brand} or another Morphit site you trust.

**Signed in with an existing Blurt account?** Then you have no 12-word phrase, and none can be made: a phrase creates keys, it can't be worked out from keys you already have. Your backup is the keyfile from the [Back up my keys](/backup-keys) page. It is locked with your {brand} password and holds your Posting key — plus your Active key, if you chose to keep it on this device. Guard it like the paper above, and don't forget the password: without it the keyfile is useless.

trade_size_limits.q: Is there a minimum or maximum trade size on {brand}?
trade_size_limits.a:
No minimum, and no real maximum. The only cap is a typo guard at one trillion, so nobody can post a nonsense number.

What limits you in practice:
• **Finding a match.** Very small and very large orders take longer to find someone willing to trade.
• **Fees.** Each listing has a small fee, so tiny trades may not be worth it.
• **Payment limits.** Banks and payment apps often have their own minimums and daily caps — check before you agree.

For a big amount, consider splitting it into a few smaller trades with the same person, so neither of you risks it all at once. This builds trust between you two, but not extra reputation: only their latest review of you counts.

rogue_operator.q: If a bad operator starts lying to users, can you shut them down?
rogue_operator.a:
**No** — and that's on purpose.

Anyone can run a Morphit site: they pay for their own server, run the open-source code and read the public blockchain. Nobody approves operators, so nobody can switch one off. We have no access to their server, there's no central gateway to block, the blockchain is public, and the software gives every operator the same rules, including the same 90% share of BLURT fees.

What we **can** do is **warn** people — on our own website, in our Matrix room (`#agorise:matrix.org`) and from the @morphit Blurt account — so you can decide which site to trust.

You can also check for yourself:
• The [Instances](/instances) page marks a site **Mismatch** when its operator account or fee addresses don't match the values on the chain.
• Each release's file fingerprints (hashes) are signed on the chain, and your browser compares them with the files the site sends. That catches a changed file on an honest server — but a hostile operator also serves the checking code and can hide a change from it.
• The stronger checks: compare what two different sites show you, or download and verify the release yourself (`docs/VERIFY-YOUR-DOWNLOAD.md`).

Why no off switch? If we could shut down a bad operator, a government could make us shut down a good one. And a better operator *should* win more users than morphit.io — that's the market working.

xmr_txid.q: What is a Monero TxID and where do I find it?
xmr_txid.a:
A Monero transaction ID (TxID, sometimes called a *hash*) is a 64-character code, using 0–9 and a–f, that names one Monero payment. To find it, open the payment in your wallet's history: the TxID is the long code in its details, usually with a copy button.

**When {brand} asks for it:** when you tell your trade partner you've paid in Monero (the **Pay now** button in chat), and when you pay a listing fee in XMR (if this site takes XMR fees). For a fee, you paste the TxID together with the payment's transaction key, so every Morphit site can check it — see "What is the Monero transaction key and why does {brand} ask for it?".

**Privacy:** a TxID is public anyway — anyone can look it up on a block explorer — and it doesn't show who you are or your balance. But it is saved with your listing on the Blurt chain, which links that one fee payment to your account. Your trade payment itself goes person to person, off Blurt. If you share its TxID in chat, it travels in your encrypted chat, which only you and your partner can read. For no Monero link at all, pay the fee in BLURT: it's the default and costs half as much.

xmr_tx_proof.q: What is the Monero transaction key and why does {brand} ask for it?
xmr_tx_proof.a:
Every Monero payment has a **transaction key**: a 64-character code (0–9, a–f) kept by the wallet that sent it. With the transaction ID and this key, anyone can check that the payment reached a given address and how much it carried. The key can't move any money.

**Why {brand} asks for it.** When you pay the listing fee in XMR, your listing carries the transaction ID and key, so every Morphit site can check the payment itself with public Monero explorers (Tor onion ones first). Nobody needs the treasury wallet's secret keys.

**Your fee address is made for your listing.** Once the treasury's main Monero address is published on the chain, each listing gets its own fee address with a hidden listing code inside. Only your transaction key reveals that code, so nobody can copy your ID and key onto their own listing, and one payment can't pay twice.

**Where to find it.**
• Monero CLI: `get_tx_key <transaction ID>`
• Monero GUI: Transactions → the payment's details → "Transaction key"
• Feather: History → right-click the payment → Show details → Copy Tx Secret Key
• Cake Wallet: tap the payment → "Transaction Key"
• Monerujo: tap the payment → "TX Key"
Only the sending wallet has it — an exchange can't give it to you.

**Privacy.** The key is published with your listing. Someone who also knows your wallet address could use it to spot the change from this payment. For the most privacy, pay from an address you haven't shared with anyone, or pay in BLURT.

**"Payment proofs" (OutProof…) no longer work.** A listing sent with one shows "fee can't be checked" — post it again with the transaction key.

morphit_mirrors.q: Why is Morphit's source mirrored to so many code hosts?
morphit_mirrors.a:
So nobody can silence the project by taking down one website. A project kept in one place can be killed in one place: a platform can suspend it, a government can force a takedown, or a host can simply disappear.

The Morphit source code (open source, AGPL-3.0) lives on more than a dozen code hosts, such as the Agorise Forgejo, GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, SourceHut, Bitbucket and Launchpad, plus IPFS, which no single host controls. If one host drops it, the other copies remain, and the license lets anyone copy, check or fork it. The full list is on the [Download page](/download).

There's nothing to get from an app store: {brand} installs straight from your browser. The mirrors are for the code.

android_sideload.q: How do I install {brand} on Android?
android_sideload.a:
Open {brand} in Chrome, Brave or another browser, tap the menu (⋮), then **Install app** or **Add to Home screen**. The icon goes on your home screen and opens full-screen like a normal app. Its pages open even without a connection (live orders need internet), and when a new version is out it asks you before switching.

There's no APK file to download, so Android's sideloading hurdles and Google's rules for Android developers don't apply. A web app installs straight from the site — no app store, and no gatekeeper who can pull it.

operator_registration.q: How does someone become a Morphit operator?
operator_registration.a:
Anyone can run a Morphit site — nobody has to approve you. The setup guide is at [Run a node](/run-a-node).

To appear as an operator, you register as one on the Blurt chain. The setup wizard can do this for you, or run `morphit-ops register`. This registration publishes a `morphit_operator_register_v1` record, signed by your relay account, that holds:
• your **operator tag** — 1 to 64 characters: lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores;
• your site's name, address and contact link;
• your **fees account**, which receives your 90% share of BLURT fees.

Tags are first come, first served and can't be changed later; tags that imitate the project's own names are refused. Re-run the command anytime to update everything except the tag.

Why it matters: registered operators are listed on the [Operators](/operators) page and in the instance directory, and other sites only accept a fee share paid to the fees account in your registration. Without it, your users' BLURT-paid orders show only on your own site. See "How do operators earn?".

operator_payouts_timing.q: When do operators get paid their fee share?
operator_payouts_timing.a:
Right away — inside the same transaction the user pays with. When someone pays a BLURT fee on your site (a listing fee, a first-message fee or a featured-slot bid), that one transaction sends 90% to your fees account and 10% to the Morphit treasury. Your share arrives as soon as the transaction is in a Blurt block, a few seconds later.

No batching, no payout schedule, no minimum to withdraw, and nobody in the middle who could hold your money.

**Three exceptions:**
• **BTC and XMR fees go 100% to the Morphit treasury.** Splitting them would need someone to hold and forward the money, which Morphit's no-custody design rules out. See "How do operators earn?".
• If your fees account is empty or not a valid account name, the whole BLURT fee goes to the treasury.
• If a fee is paid from your fees account itself, the whole fee goes to the treasury, because Blurt can't send money from an account to itself.

It's all on the chain, so you can check every payment yourself.

operator_moderation.q: Can operators block or ban specific users from their instance?
operator_moderation.a:
Yes, on their own site only. An operator can block an account with the `morphit-ops` moderation tools. The site then stops showing that account's listings — in the orderbook, on their profile, in featured slots, in RSS feeds and in the live feed. If the blocked person signs in there, a banner tells them they're blocked on this site, with the reason if one was given.

What a block does **not** do:
• Touch the blockchain. Their orders are still there and still show on every other Morphit site (see [Instances](/instances)).
• Touch their funds, keys or account.
• Stop them trading. They can use any other site, or run their own.

Blocks aren't secret: the site's public data lists every account it has blocked, and why. And a block can be undone at any time.

Operators use this against spam and abuse — for example, listings for goods or services that would harm someone. #donoharm

chat_identity_key.q: Do I need to set up a separate key to use chat?
chat_identity_key.a:
No. Your chat key is made automatically from your Blurt posting key the first time you open chat. There's nothing extra to create, back up or lose.

How it works:
• Your browser turns your posting key into a separate chat key pair.
• The public half is published on the Blurt chain once, in the background, so others can encrypt messages to you.
• The private half never leaves your browser. It's rebuilt the same way every time, so a page refresh or a new device gives you the same key.

The trade-off: anyone who gets your posting key — for example by stealing your 12-word phrase — can also read all your past chats, and your new ones until you change your posting key. They could already pose as you, so the thing to protect doesn't change: keep your 12-word phrase and your password safe.

syndicate_trade_announcement.q: What is the "Syndicate my order" checkbox?
syndicate_trade_announcement.a:
When you post an order, you can tick **Syndicate my order to the Blurt blog**. Right after your order goes up, {brand} posts a short announcement of it to your own Blurt blog, with a link back to the order on {brand}. It's tagged #morphit, so people browsing that tag can find it.

The post is signed with *your* posting key — not the operator's or the project's — so it's genuinely from you, and it's a normal post on your blog. Upvotes on it can earn you BLURT.

There's also a one-time option: **Announce my first trade to the @morphit community**. It's off unless you turn it on, on the order form or in Settings. If it's on, a short first-trade post goes to the @morphit community when you leave your first feedback. After that, Settings instead lets you tick the blog box on every new order by default.

offline_caching.a:
Partly. Once {brand} has loaded, its pages, design, fonts and icons are saved on your device. If your connection drops — a tunnel, an elevator, bad wi-fi — you can still open pages and read things like this FAQ.

Anything live needs a connection:
• the current orderbook, profiles and prices;
• sending orders, chat messages and feedback.

Some privacy browsers, such as Tor Browser, turn this offline saving off. {brand} still works there (except at Tor Browser's "Safest" level, which turns off JavaScript); it just loads everything fresh.

lock_vs_signout.q: What's the difference between Lock Session and Sign Out?
lock_vs_signout.a:
**Lock session** wipes your keys from memory but keeps the encrypted copy on this device. Next time you open {brand} here, you unlock with just your password — no seed phrase needed.

**Sign out** wipes your keys from memory *and* deletes the encrypted copy from this device. To get back in, you need your 12-word seed phrase, your keyfile or your Blurt key.

Use **Lock** on your own device when you step away. Use **Sign out** on a public or shared computer, or before handing the device to someone else.

Two details:
• Lock only differs from Sign out if this device remembers you: you chose "Password (fast)" when you created your account, or ticked "remember me" when you signed in. Otherwise nothing was saved, so both end the same way.
• Locking by hand also clears your unsent drafts. The automatic idle lock keeps them.

login_password_vs_key.q: Why does {brand} ask for my posting key when I log in, instead of the password I set?
login_password_vs_key.a:
Your key (or your 12-word seed phrase) is your real login. The password only unlocks a copy of your key that {brand} saved, encrypted, in *this one browser*, so you don't have to paste the key every time.

So which one you're asked for depends on whether that saved copy is here:
• **You used Sign out:** the saved copy was deleted on purpose, for safety, so {brand} asks for your key again. That's normal, not a bug.
• **You only locked, or closed the tab:** if this device remembers you, the copy is still here, so you just type your password.
• **New computer, browser or phone:** your key was never saved there, so you need it the first time.

Your key is never kept on a server, so a password alone can't unlock a new device. Tip: to keep the quick password login, use **Lock** instead of **Sign out**.

auto_lock_timeout.q: When does my session auto-lock if I walk away?
auto_lock_timeout.a:
By default after **9 hours** without activity. That's long on purpose: you can walk away to cook dinner and come back to your trades without signing in again.

To change it, go to **Settings → Utility → Auto-lock after idle** (shown when this device remembers you) and pick 15 or 30 minutes, 1, 4, 9 or 24 hours, or **Never** (you lock it yourself).

Typing, clicking, scrolling, moving the mouse, touching the screen, or coming back to the {brand} tab all count as activity and restart the clock.

When time runs out, your session locks — like **Lock session** in the avatar menu, except your unsent drafts are kept. Your keys are wiped from memory; if this device remembers you, unlock again with your password.

push_notifications_privacy.q: How do push notifications work with my privacy?
push_notifications_privacy.a:
Push notifications tell you when someone messages you, leaves you feedback, or outbids your featured slot — even when the {brand} tab is closed. To do that, a "push service" has to hold each alert until your device picks it up.

**The honest part: your browser picks that push service, not us.** Chrome and most Chromium browsers use Google, Firefox uses Mozilla, Safari uses Apple, and Edge on Windows uses Microsoft. {brand} has no way to point it at a different server.

What that service sees is metadata: that your browser got a push from this site, and when. It never sees the content — every push is end-to-end encrypted, so it can't read your messages or orders.

**What this site keeps for push:** your account name, the push address your browser gave you, your language and the alert types you muted — until you turn push off or the address stops working. Each alert (for example "@bob sent you a message") is also kept for about an hour after it's sent, then deleted. Not your browser's user-agent. It only sends to the browser makers' push services, or ones the operator added.

If that metadata bothers you, turn push off. You still get badges on your avatar, the tab icon and the title while {brand} is open — those never leave your browser.

**What we removed:** older versions had a "Self-hosted only" option. It did nothing — Chrome still used Google. It's gone. We'd like to offer a real choice of push server one day (UnifiedPush).

user_hide_accounts.q: Can I hide orders from specific users?
user_hide_accounts.a:
Yes. On a computer or tablet, every order in the orderbook has a small hide button (it isn't shown on narrow phone screens). Click it and confirm, and you won't see that account's orders any more — your chats with them are hidden too. They are never told.

When you are signed in, your hidden list is saved with your account settings, encrypted so only you can read it. It follows you when you sign in on another device or another Morphit site.

To undo it, go to **Settings → Hidden accounts** and unhide one person, or everyone at once. When the orderbook has hidden orders, a note at the top says how many, with a **Show anyway** button to peek without unhiding.

Hiding only changes what *you* see. It doesn't ban anyone: their orders still exist, and everyone else still sees them.

what_is_reputation.a:
After a trade, each side can rate the other from 1 to 5 stars and add a short comment — once per order. Reviews are saved on the Blurt blockchain, so they are public and permanent. Nobody, not even the site, can edit or delete them.

Each trader's profile shows their reviews, a star breakdown and a **reputation score from 0 to 5** (for example 4.06). The same score sits on their orders, next to how many trades they have completed.

How the score works, in plain words:

• Newer reviews count more. A review loses half its weight each year.
• A trader with only a few reviews stays close to a neutral 3.0, so one glowing review can't make a stranger look like a veteran.
• A long, recent, good record earns a small bonus. Lots of trading can never rescue bad ratings.
• Only reviews from a real trade partner count. Fake-looking patterns are left out.

**Your reputation is everything.** {brand} has no escrow and no referee. Your track record is what lets a stranger trust you, so treat every trade as if it matters — it does.

how_to_build_high_reputation.q: How do I build a high reputation score on {brand}?
how_to_build_high_reputation.a:
There's no shortcut: real trades, done well, over time.

**What raises your score**

• **Finish real trades and get reviewed.** A review only counts if it comes from someone you really chatted with (at least 2 messages each way, over at least 15 minutes) and names an order you two traded on whose listing fee was paid.
• **Stay active.** Newer reviews count more — each review loses half its weight per year. The small bonus for a good record also halves for every 6 months without a new review.
• **Be good on both sides.** Your profile shows your rating as a buyer and as a seller separately.
• **Review back.** When a trade goes well, leave your partner an honest review too.

**What doesn't work**

• Reviewing yourself — it's rejected.
• Fake accounts, two friends swapping 5-star reviews, one account aiming most of its reviews at one person, or a group piling bad reviews on someone. These patterns are flagged and left out.
• Lots of reviews from one person — only their latest review of you counts.
• Reviews that don't name a trade. They show on your profile but don't count.

New accounts carry a 🌱 badge until they have 4 completed trades. That's normal — start small.

Anyone can check your score: each site publishes a public reputation receipt (for the technically curious: `/v1/accounts/<name>/reputation-receipt`) that lists every review about you, whether it counted, and why not if it didn't.

how_to_leave_feedback.q: How do I leave feedback after a trade?
how_to_leave_feedback.a:
When the trade is done, you can review the other person from two places:

• **In the chat** for that order. After a payment has been marked as sent, a **Mark this trade complete** card appears under the messages.
• **In [My Orders](/my/orders)**, for orders you posted. Click **Mark complete / review** and pick who you traded with.

Choose 1 to 5 stars, add a comment if you like (up to 256 characters), and submit. If it's your own order, this also marks it complete and takes it off the orderbook.

You can only review someone you really talked with: at least 2 messages each way, spread over at least 15 minutes. The review is signed with your posting key, so there's no password prompt. {brand} charges nothing for it; Blurt takes its usual tiny network fee from your liquid BLURT. It shows on their profile in about a minute.

feedback_reply.q: Can I respond to a review someone left about me?
feedback_reply.a:
Yes. Open your own profile, find the review under **Reviews received**, and click **Reply**. You get one public reply per review (up to 256 characters). It shows right under the review, so readers see both sides.

Replies are saved on the blockchain like reviews, so they're permanent. Use them to explain calmly, not to argue. Nobody can edit or delete the original review — not you, not the site.

reviews_given_visibility.q: Who can see the reviews I've left for other traders?
reviews_given_visibility.a:
Everyone. Every profile has a **Reviews given** tab listing each review that person has left, with a link to the order it was about.

That's on purpose: how you rate others is part of your own reputation. If someone hands out 1-star reviews that nobody else agrees with, readers can see the pattern and judge for themselves.

private_key_warning.q: Why did {brand} warn me about a private key in my message?
private_key_warning.a:
Because it spotted something that looks like a private key or a seed phrase. {brand} checks what you type in chat messages, order terms, review comments and replies to reviews for:

• private keys in the common 'WIF' format (like your Blurt posting or active key),
• 64-character hex keys (such as Monero private keys),
• 12 or more seed-phrase words in a row.

A match turns red, and a warning pops up before anything is sent. A private key is the key to a wallet: whoever sees it can take everything in it, forever. No real support person, admin or trade partner will ever ask for one.

If you choose **Send truncated anyway**, {brand} shortens the key on your device to its first 6 and last 4 characters, so the full secret never leaves. Other order fields and your profile get the same shortening automatically, without the pop-up.

new_trader_badge.q: What does the 'New trader' label mean?
new_trader_badge.a:
It's the little 🌱 sprout next to a trader's name. It means the account has fewer than 4 completed trades on record — counting only orders whose listing fee was paid (plus a trader's free first order), and leaving out trades between accounts flagged as working together.

They might be brand new, or just someone who rarely trades. It isn't a red flag — everyone starts here. If you trade with a newcomer, start with a small amount. Afterwards, an honest review helps the next person decide.

profile_pages.q: What's on a user's profile page?
profile_pages.a:
Every profile lives at /@username, and anyone can view it without signing in. From top to bottom:

• **Who they are** — their picture (or a pattern made from their account name), display name, a short bio, and links to their Nostr, website or streaming page if they added any.
• **Reputation** — their 0–5 score, number of ratings, average stars, a 5-to-1 star breakdown, separate buyer and seller ratings, and when they last traded.
• **Tabs** — *Reviews received* (with any replies), *Reviews given*, and *Active orders*, oldest first so the ones closest to expiring come first.

profile_own_vs_others.q: What changes when I'm viewing my own profile vs someone else's?
profile_own_vs_others.a:
On your own profile you also see:

• your balance card,
• a **Trade history** tab with your completed trades,
• a **Reply** button under each review you haven't answered yet.

On someone else's profile you see a **Message @name** button instead.

Order pages work the same way. On your own order you get **Edit** (only in the first 15 minutes after posting) and **Cancel this order** — or **Re-list this order** once it has expired or been cancelled. On someone else's live order you see the **Message @name** button, with a short note about using it to agree on payment.

share_order_link.q: Can I share a link to my order?
share_order_link.a:
Yes. Open the order and copy the address from your browser's address bar — it ends in /@username/ followed by the order's code (like order-k3x9…). Anyone can open it without signing in and see the full offer: price, payment methods, location, terms, and who posted it with their reputation.

Share it anywhere — Nostr, a chat, a forum. The link stays the same if you edit the order. Once the order is completed, cancelled or expired, the link still opens and simply shows that status.

forward_secrecy.a:
No. {brand} chat does not have forward secrecy. That's a deliberate trade-off — here's the honest version.

**How a message is locked.** Each message gets a fresh one-time key, mixed with your chat key and your partner's. Only the two of you can open it, and your partner can tell it really came from you. Your chat key is made from your Blurt posting key and stays the same until that key changes.

**If a key is ever stolen.** Anyone who later gets your partner's chat key can read every message ever sent to them. By default you keep a copy of what you send, so your own key opens those too. You can stop keeping that copy (⋮ → Chat Security), but your partner's key still opens them, and the encrypted messages stay on the chain forever.

**Why we chose this.**

• Any message opens on its own — out of order, years later, on a new device — with no setup and nothing to pair.
• Every device signed in to your account is the same chat identity.
• The crypto code stays small and easy to audit.
• Someone holding your posting key can already post, chat and publish a new chat key as you, so per-message keys would protect little.

**If that's not enough for you** — for talks that could be investigated years from now — use a dedicated messenger such as Matrix/Element, Session or Signal. {brand} chat is for arranging a trade.

chat_dispute_recourse.q: If I disagree with my counterparty later, can I prove what we agreed to in chat?
chat_dispute_recourse.a:
Partly. {brand} chat is stored on the Blurt blockchain, so nobody can edit or quietly delete what was said, and you can scroll back to the very first message. (If you stopped keeping your own copy in ⋮ → Chat Security, you can't reread your own messages after you leave — your partner still can.)

**What you can show others.** Each message is a blockchain transaction signed by the sender's account, with a time and a transaction ID. Anyone can look these up on a Blurt block explorer to confirm *who* sent a message to *whom* and *when*. The chain holds only the encrypted form, so it can't prove the *wording* to an outsider.

**Export.** Open the chat's ⋮ menu and choose **Export chat**. You get a PDF of every message the two of you ever exchanged, in every chat about every order, each with its UTC time and transaction ID, plus a page explaining how to check them. It's an ordinary, editable file — a tidy record for a mediator or court, not proof of the wording on its own.

**What it can't do.** {brand} has no escrow and nobody who settles disputes, so evidence can't force anyone to pay — see 'Why no Escrow or Arbitration service?'. How much weight a court or mediator gives it depends on where you are.

**Tip:** before anyone sends money, write the exact asset, amount, payment method and any special terms in the chat.

chat_vs_feedback_visibility.q: What's public and what's private about my trades on {brand}?
chat_vs_feedback_visibility.a:
Some of it is private and some is public — on purpose.

**Private (only you and your trade partner can read it):**

• **What you say in chat** — prices, payment details, addresses, meeting places, phone numbers. Messages are end-to-end encrypted; operators and anyone watching the blockchain see only scrambled text. See 'Are my chats private?'.

**Public (anyone can read it):**

• **Your orders**, including prices and terms.
• **Reviews** — stars, comments and replies. Each review names the order it's about, so it publicly links the two accounts (@squirrel and @scooby) to that trade. See 'Who can see the reviews I've left for other traders?'.
• **Everything about a chat except the words:** who talked to whom, when, about which order, roughly how long each message was, and how far each of you has read (read receipts).

All of it is saved on the Blurt blockchain, and nothing saved there can be deleted. The only difference is who can read it.

Why? Chat stays private so payment details don't leak. Reviews stay public so anyone can check a reputation. If even the fact that you talked must stay hidden, use a separate secure messenger for that part.

how_morphit_protects_me.q: How does {brand} protect me from scammers and stop them from getting my private keys or personal info?
how_morphit_protects_me.a:
Mostly by having little worth stealing, plus a few safety nets.

**Little to steal.** {brand} never holds your coins, and your private keys are made on your device and never sent to the site. No email, phone number or ID is asked for, and IP addresses are kept only in memory, to limit abuse. A hacked server holds none of your keys and no identities — though it could serve tampered page code, so use sites you trust.

**Key guard.** Paste something that looks like a private key or seed phrase into a chat, order or review and you get a red warning; send anyway and only its first 6 and last 4 characters go out. See 'Why did {brand} warn me about a private key in my message?'.

**Spam gates.** A stranger who isn't answering one of your orders must pay a small BLURT fee to message you first, unless you wrote to them first. Blocked accounts can't reach you. See 'How does {brand} stop spam and unsolicited messages from strangers?'.

**Hard-to-fake reviews.** A review counts only if the reviewer really chatted with you and names an order one of you paid a listing fee for — and only their latest review of you counts. See 'How does {brand} stop fake reviews?'.

**A locked-down site.** What you send is checked, and pages run only the site's own code. See 'Is {brand} vulnerable to hacking, data theft, or takedowns?'.

No software can stop a scammer talking you into a bad deal — see 'What scams should I watch out for on {brand}?'.

chat_anti_spam.q: How does {brand} stop spam and unsolicited messages from strangers?
chat_anti_spam.a:
Three layers keep strangers from flooding you, while normal trade chat stays free.

**1. Block.** You can block any account; its messages to you are then simply not delivered. A new account still has to get past the two layers below.

**2. A small first-contact fee.** The first message to someone you have never chatted with costs 5 BLURT, paid once per person (90% to the site operator, 10% to the Morphit treasury). It is free if the two of you have already exchanged a message, or if you are writing about one of their live orders — posting an order is an invitation.

The fee doubles for each extra stranger a sender contacts within 5 minutes: 5, 10, 20, 40… up to 640 BLURT each. Eight strangers in 5 minutes cost 1,275 BLURT. After 5 quiet minutes it is back to 5.

**3. Limits until you reply.** Until you answer someone, they can send you at most 50 messages, and at most 20 unanswered new people can start chats with you in 24 hours. Your first reply lifts both limits for that person.

These numbers are fixed in the code and the same on every Morphit site; operators can't change them.

chat_inbox_features.q: How does the chat inbox work? Can I mute or unmute someone?
chat_inbox_features.a:
Tap **Chat** in the header to open your inbox. It works like email: **one card per discussion**, not one per person.

Talk with the same trader about three orders and you get three cards. Each card has a "RE:" line naming the order and its state — Live, Canceled, Expired or Paid — or "RE: -" if the chat isn't about an order.

Opening a card marks **only that one** read, on all your devices. Unread cards have a green border, and the badge on your avatar (top right), the browser tab and the site icon show the unread count. **Mark all as read** clears them all. Read marks are saved publicly on the chain: anyone can see up to when you read a chat with someone, never what it said.

Three tabs:
• **Inbox** — everything lands here.
• **Starred** — tap the star on a card (or in the conversation's ⋮ menu) to keep it here; tap again to move it back.
• **Archived** — tap **Archive** to file a discussion away; it stops counting as unread, and a new message brings it back. **Restore** returns it to the Inbox.

Starred and Archived sync between your devices, encrypted; the other person never sees them.

**Mute = Block.** In a conversation, open ⋮ → Block: that account can no longer message you. To unmute, go to **Settings → Blocked accounts** and tap Unblock. Blocks are public — see 'If I block someone, will they know?'.

notifications_overview.q: How does {brand} let me know when something happens — a new message, an order filling, feedback arriving?
notifications_overview.a:
{brand} tells you about new things in a few ways. The quiet ones are always on; the louder ones are your choice, in **Settings → Notifications**.

**Always on (no permission needed):**
• The browser tab title starts with the unread count, like "(3)".
• The site icon in the tab gets a small dot with the count.
• If you installed {brand} as an app, its icon gets a badge (where your system supports it).
These work while you are signed in and unlocked.

**Your choice (off until you turn them on):**
• **Desktop notifications** — a pop-up when the {brand} tab isn't in front. Your browser asks permission the first time one would show.
• **Sound** — a short chime.
• **Vibration** — a short buzz, on phones that support it.
• **Push notifications** — alerts even when {brand} is closed. They travel through your browser maker's push service; see 'How do push notifications work with my privacy?'.

**What you're told about:** orders and trade steps, chat messages, and feedback. All three are on by default; switch off any you don't want.

**Quiet hours** and **Silence everything** stop pop-ups and sounds. Push notifications still appear (browsers require it), but silently.

**While you're away:** if this site offers it, {brand} can also send a short note to an app you use, like email or Telegram. See "How do offline notifications work, and how is my address kept private?".

For the chat inbox, see "How does the chat inbox work? Can I mute or unmute someone?".

offline_notifications.q: How do offline notifications work, and how is my address kept private?
offline_notifications.a:
If someone sends you a chat message while you're away, {brand} can send you a short note on an app you already use, so you don't miss it. It's off until you turn it on, in **Settings → Offline Notifications**.

**Turning it on.** Pick one of the apps this site offers: Matrix, Session, XMPP, Telegram or email. Each site chooses which ones it offers. Type your address for that app and we send a code to it. Type the code in, and it's on. For Telegram it works the other way round: you send our bot a code, and the button does that for you. The code proves the address is yours, so nobody can sign up someone else.

**What the note says.** Only "Someone just sent you a chat message on {brand}", with a link. It never says who wrote or what they wrote. The link opens that conversation, and only for you; anyone else who gets hold of it gets nothing. It stops working after 7 days.

**When it comes.** Not right away: 10 to 60 minutes after the message, and always on the hour, quarter past, half past or quarter to. (Why is explained below.) You don't get one if you're already on the site, or once you've read the conversation or replied. You get one note per conversation until you look at it, and at most one a day from someone you've never written to.

**How your address is kept private.**
• It is stored encrypted, and the key that unlocks it is kept apart from the database. A copy of the database alone opens nothing.
• It is never shown to anyone. It isn't on your profile, it isn't shown to the people you trade with, and it's never shared with other sites. Once it's saved, even you only see "On".
• It is left out of the site's backups and logs.
• Only you can add or change it, because every change is signed with your key.
• **Turn off** removes one app; **Delete all my addresses** removes everything. Your address is deleted right away. If the site stops offering an app, the addresses saved for it are deleted, or the card shows a button to delete yours.

**The honest part.**
• The app that brings you the note can read it, the same as any message you get there: it can see that you use this site and when a note came, never who wrote or what. Only Session encrypts it from end to end. That's why notes go out after a random wait, at times shared by everyone: from the moment one arrives, it's much harder to tell which chat message it was about.
• To deliver a note, the service the site sends it through (its email, Matrix, XMPP, Session or Telegram account) has to be given your address, as with any message sent to you.
• The people who run this site run the server that holds the key, so you're trusting them with your address, as with any service you give an address to. Nothing on the site shows it to them, but whoever controls the server could get at it.

**Tip:** for the most privacy, use an address you don't use for anything else. Session needs no phone number or email address at all.

chat_key_changed.q: What does "We couldn't safely send" mean?
chat_key_changed.a:
The first time you message someone, {brand} remembers their chat key in your browser. Before every later message it checks that the key your site reports still matches. If something doesn't add up, the message is held back instead of sent.

**Most common: their key changed.** That happens when your partner resets their keys — or when someone is trying to read your messages. Open ⋮ → **Verify peer** and compare the safety number with them another way (a call, in person). Accept the new key only if the numbers match; until then nothing is sent. Their older messages stay readable but are marked unverified.

**Other cases** — the key record looks tampered with, is older than one you've already seen, is missing on the chain, or is garbled. These point to a broken or out-of-date indexer, not to your partner.

**What to do:**
• Retry once — it may be a hiccup.
• Switch to another Morphit site (link at the bottom of the page); each runs its own indexer.
• Ask your partner, another way, whether they reset their keys.

These checks read the chain through your site's own servers, so they catch a broken indexer, not a lying operator. The safety number protects you there: compare it once with each partner.

See also 'How does {brand} chat work?' and 'Are my chats private?'.

order_fee_rejected.q: My order isn't showing up. What does the fee status mean?
order_fee_rejected.a:
An order shows on the public orderbook only after its listing fee is confirmed. **My orders** shows each order's fee status:

• **Visible in orderbook** — fee confirmed. All done.
• **Verified (attested)** — a BTC or XMR fee the block explorers couldn't answer for, vouched for by two independent community members instead. Your order is live.
• **Awaiting attestation** — a BTC or XMR fee still being checked. A paid fee is usually confirmed within minutes of your payment confirming on its own chain.
• **Waiting for your BTC fee** — pay the BTC fee to the address shown for that order; it goes live once the payment confirms.
• **Not yet verified** — not checked yet. Wait a little.
• **Fee payment not received** — no matching fee was found: the payment failed, went to the wrong place, or the transaction ID was wrong.
• **Fee underpaid** — the fee was too small. A BLURT fee goes up when you have many live orders or posted many in the last 24 hours.
• **Payment already used** — that BTC or XMR payment already paid for another order. One payment pays for one order.
• **Fee can't be checked** — post the XMR order again, this time with the transaction key.

If an order is stuck on a "Not in orderbook" status, cancel it and post a new one with the right fee.

signup_stuck.q: Signup isn't working. What do these errors mean?
signup_stuck.a:
This site's relay creates your Blurt account and pays the fee for you (about 102 BLURT), so it has limits against abuse. What the messages mean:

• **"Verifying you're human…" takes long, or "Human verification failed"** — your browser solves a small puzzle (Altcha). Close other tabs, refresh and try again.
• **"You've made too many attempts. Try again in an hour."** — too many sign-up tries from your internet connection in the last hour. Shared Wi-Fi counts everyone on it. Wait, or use another network.
• **"You recently created an account. Please wait…"** — signups from one connection must be spaced apart (an hour, by default).
• **"You've reached today's signup limit"** — your connection's daily limit. Try tomorrow.
• **"This instance has reached its daily signup limit"** — the whole site's daily cap. It resets at midnight UTC, or try another Morphit site.
• **"Signups are temporarily unavailable"**, **"temporarily out of funds"** or **"Registration is paused"** — the operator has paused signups or needs to top up the relay. Try later, or another site.
• **"Your signup token expired or was already used"** — often your connection changed (say, Wi-Fi to mobile data). Refresh and retry.
• **"That name was just taken"**, **"isn't allowed"** or **"is reserved"** — pick another name. Names are 3–16 characters: lowercase letters, digits and single dashes, starting with a letter, no dots.
• **"Registration was rejected"** — try a different name.
• **"The Blurt network did not confirm in time"** — wait a minute and retry with the same name.

See also 'What do I need to sign up?', and after signing up, 'What is the welcome bonus and how do I earn it?'.

verified_chat_badge.q: What is the "Verified chat" badge on a review?
verified_chat_badge.a:
A small green check on a review. It means the reviewer and the trader really talked in chat before the review was posted:
• at least 2 messages from each side,
• spread over at least 15 minutes,
• and the two haven't been caught swapping top reviews with each other.

Today every new review needs this — a review without such a chat is refused — so all new reviews carry the badge. Some older reviews don't.

**What it doesn't prove:** that the two accounts are different people. One patient person with two accounts can chat with themselves.

**Why not check IP addresses?** That would mean collecting them, VPNs and Tor would beat it, and honest people on shared Wi-Fi would be wrongly flagged.

**How to use it:** as one clue among several. A reviewer with an older account who has reviewed many different traders tells you more than the badge alone.

feedback_suppressed.q: Why are some reviews greyed out as 'not counted toward rating'?
feedback_suppressed.a:
These suppressed reviews still show, but they don't count toward the star rating or review count at the top of the profile. They're greyed out and marked "Not counted toward the rating".

A review doesn't count when:
• **Same maker:** both accounts were created by the same account (not a Morphit site's signup service) and became active within 5 minutes of each other.
• **Back-scratching:** two accounts gave each other 3 or more top reviews (4.8★+ on average) within 7 days and reviewed nobody else.
• **Pile-on:** 3 or more accounts left low reviews (2★ or less on average) for one trader within 7 days, and those accounts started around the same time and review almost no one else.
• **One favourite:** at least 80% of a reviewer's reviews (5 or more in 30 days), averaging 4.5★+, go to one trader.
• It isn't linked to an order, so it can't be tied to a trade.
• The same reviewer reviewed this trader again later — only their latest review counts.

**Why show them at all?** The chain is public, so hiding them would only pretend. Greyed out says: this exists, but it doesn't count.

**Wrongly flagged?** The checks aren't perfect. The operator of the site you're viewing can clear a flag for a pair — contact them.

See also "How does {brand}'s reputation system work?".

block_privacy.q: If I block someone, will they know?
block_privacy.a:
**{brand} never tells someone you blocked them** — telling a stalker who blocked them only helps them get around it. But a block isn't secret.

**What they see:** if they message you, their message shows as not accepted for delivery ("the recipient may not be taking messages from you right now"), without saying why.

**What's public:** a block is saved on the Blurt chain, like everything on {brand}. Anyone who reads the chain — or looks up your block list through a site's public data feed — can see whom you blocked and when. {brand}'s screens just don't point it out.

**If they make a new account:** your block covers only the account you blocked. A new one must pay the first-contact fee (5 BLURT and up, doubling if they rush) — unless they write about one of your live orders, which is free. Also, at most 20 unanswered new people can start chats with you per 24 hours. You can block the new account too.

**Changed your mind?** Go to **Settings → Blocked accounts** and tap Unblock. That's public too, and messages sent while they were blocked are not delivered later.

See also "How does {brand} stop spam and unsolicited messages from strangers?".

what_is_mana.a:
On Blurt, Mana is your voting power. It only decides how much weight your upvotes carry. Think of a stamina bar: each vote uses a little, and it refills by about 20% a day. The more Blurt Power (BP) you hold, the more your votes count.

Mana does **not** pay for anything you do. (On Steem and Hive, "Resource Credits" pay for actions; Blurt dropped that.) On Blurt, every action costs a small fee in BLURT, taken from your liquid (unstaked) balance: a transfer, a post, and on {brand} an order, a review or an encrypted chat message. Mana only matters for voting.

So the rule is simple: keep a little liquid BLURT in your account and your actions go through. You never have to wait for Mana to refill before you trade. Receiving BLURT is free, so topping up is easy.

node_minimum_requirements.q: What are the minimum hardware requirements to run a Morphit node?
node_minimum_requirements.a:
Modest. An old PC or laptop, a small mini-PC, a cheap rented server (VPS) or a Raspberry Pi will do, as long as it meets these minimums:

• **CPU:** 2 cores or more (64-bit x86 or ARM).
• **Memory:** 4 GB of RAM or more.
• **Disk:** 80 GB free or more. An SSD is best.
• **System:** Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, or a flavor built on it (Linux Mint 22, Pop!_OS 24.04, Zorin OS 17). The one-command installer refuses anything else, including Debian and older Ubuntu.
• **Power and internet:** a machine that stays on.

The installer checks your machine before it starts and tells you if anything falls short.

**What you don't need:**

• Your own blockchain node. Morphit reads the Blurt network through public servers.
• A static IP. At home, the installer keeps your domain pointed at you even when your address changes (dynamic DNS).
• A domain, if you choose Tor-only. Your site then lives at a `.onion` address.
• A data center. But a normal (clearnet) site run from home will expose your home IP address to every visitor. A Tor-only site does not.

One cost to know: your relay pays about 102 BLURT for every account it creates, so a site that signs up many people can lose money if very few people on it are actually trading.

iphone_install.q: Can I use {brand} on my iPhone or iPad?
iphone_install.a:
Yes. {brand} is a web app (a PWA), so there is nothing to get from the App Store and no jailbreak.

To put it on your Home Screen:
1. Open this site in **Safari**.
2. Tap **Share** (the square with an arrow pointing up).
3. Tap **Add to Home Screen**.
4. Tap **Add**.

The new icon opens {brand} full screen, like an app. Notifications on iPhone and iPad need iOS 16.4 or newer, and work only from the Home Screen icon.

block_explorer.q: Is there a block explorer for {brand}?
block_explorer.a:
Yes. Go to [the explorer](/explorer) to look up any Blurt account, transaction or block. It is public and needs no account. {brand}'s own actions (orders, reviews, chat messages, which stay encrypted, and more) are labelled in plain words, so you can tell what each one is.

Payments in other coins happen on their own blockchains. When a transaction ID for one of them appears in a chat, {brand} links it to an outside explorer for that coin, for example mempool.space for Bitcoin and xmrchain.net for Monero. The site's operator can change these links.

public_api.q: Can I build a block explorer or aggregator on top of Morphit's data?
public_api.a:
Yes, and it is free. Every Morphit instance serves the same read-only public API under `/v1/*`: no API key, no signup. Only the hostname changes.

• **Reference:** `docs/API.md` in the source lists every endpoint, for example `/v1/orderbook` (live updates at `/v1/orderbook/stream`), `/v1/orders/:account`, `/v1/accounts/:account/feedback`, `/v1/instances` and `/v1/health`. RSS, Atom and JSON feeds live under `/rss/orderbook`.
• **Stability:** documented `/v1` fields are never renamed or removed without a new `/v2`. New fields can appear, so ignore ones you don't know.
• **Rate limits:** by default 120 requests a minute per IP for lists and 600 for single-record lookups. Each operator can change these. Going over returns `429` with a `Retry-After` header.
• **Writing:** the API doesn't change data. Orders, reviews and chat are Blurt transactions you sign yourself; an instance only passes a signed transaction on (`POST /v1/broadcast`).
• **Chat:** messages are on-chain but encrypted. Only the two people in the chat can read them.

For heavy use, run your own instance (see `RUN-A-MORPHIT-NODE.md`): no rate limits, and no dependence on someone else's server. Use `/v1/instances` to find other instances and spread your load.

All of this data is on the public Blurt chain anyway. The API just saves you from building your own indexer.

what_is_featured_slot.q: What is the featured slot and how does the auction work?
what_is_featured_slot.a:
Featured slots put up to **3** orders in a highlighted spot at the top of the orderbook and on the home page of **this site**. Each site runs its own, so a bid here only buys space here.

**How to bid.** In [My orders](/my/orders), pick one of your live orders whose listing fee is confirmed, and choose 6, 24 or 72 hours. You pay the site's hourly price times the hours, in BLURT. Each operator sets their own price, and the form shows the total before you pay. 90% goes to the site's operator and 10% to the Morphit treasury.

**Who gets the slots.** Bids rank by BLURT paid per hour; at the same rate, the earlier bid wins. Because the form pays the site's current price, slots usually go first come, first served. If all 3 are taken, your bid waits and shows when a slot frees up. Your hours start counting as soon as the bid is recorded, even while it waits. To push someone out, a bid must pay at least 1 BLURT an hour or 5% more than them, whichever is bigger; the form checks this before you pay.

**No refunds.** The BLURT goes out with the bid and is not returned. See 'What happens to my featured slot if someone outbids me?'

featured_slot_displaced.q: What happens to my featured slot if someone outbids me?
featured_slot_displaced.a:
Your bid stays on record, but it drops out of view. Nothing is refunded.

{brand} shows the 3 bids paying the most BLURT per hour. If a new bid beats the lowest of the 3 by at least 1 BLURT an hour or 5% (whichever is bigger), that lowest bid drops to 4th place and leaves the featured spot. If a bid above yours ends while your hours are still running, yours comes back. Your hours keep counting the whole time: you paid for a chance at the slot during those hours, not for guaranteed visibility.

**What helps:**

• **Outbid alerts.** If you turned on push notifications, {brand} tells you when you're pushed out, with a link to the order in My orders. My orders also marks the bid "Outranked".
• **No last-second sniping.** When a new bid comes in and a top-3 bid ends within 5 minutes, that bid gets 5 more minutes. This can happen up to 6 times per bid (30 minutes in all), so you have time to respond.
• **Look first.** Before bidding, check what the current slots pay, and prefer shorter bids when competition is high.

verify_peer_fingerprint.q: How can I be sure no one is reading my chats? (Verify safety number)
verify_peer_fingerprint.a:
{brand} chats are end-to-end encrypted: messages are locked on your device, and only you and your partner can open them.

There is one weak spot. The first time you chat with someone, your browser trusts the chat key your site's server says is theirs. A dishonest server could slip in its own key and read along. **The safety number lets you rule that out.** If your partner's key changes later, nothing is sent to the new key until you check the new number and accept it (see 'What does "We couldn't safely send" mean?').

**How to check:**
1. Open the chat and tap ⋮ → **Verify peer**.
2. You see 60 digits in 12 groups of 5. Your partner opens the same screen.
3. Compare the digits by voice call, in person, or another channel you both already trust. **Not in this chat.**
4. If every digit matches, nobody swapped a key. If even one differs, treat the chat as compromised and stop.

**What it can't catch:** the wrong person on the call (you must recognise them), a hacked phone, or a dishonest copy of the app itself.

Checking is optional and posts nothing to the chain. The number is made from public keys only, and faking a match is far out of reach.

qr_login.q: What is QR login and is it safe?
qr_login.a:
QR login signs you in to {brand} on a computer using your phone, without typing your seed phrase.

**How it works:** on the computer, choose **Sign in with your phone via QR**. A one-time code appears; it works for 5 minutes. On your phone (signed in and unlocked), tap your avatar → **Sign in to another device** and scan the code. Your phone shows the website's address. Tap **Yes, that was me** only if you just opened that site yourself.

**Why it's safe:** your keys never leave your phone. The code is only a request, so a screenshot of it is useless without your phone saying yes. The server just passes along a sealed message it can't read or fake.

**Watch out:** read the website address on your phone carefully. A fake site can look almost the same (a 1 instead of an l). If you didn't just open it, tap **No, I didn't**.

**Good to know:** the computer is read-only. You can browse and see your orders and profile there, but to post, send messages, leave reviews or read encrypted chats, use your phone. If you lose your phone, sign in with your written seed phrase.

what_is_usdt.a:
USDT (Tether) is a stablecoin: a crypto token made to stay worth about 1 US dollar. It is issued by the company Tether. People use it to hold dollar value without leaving crypto.

On {brand} you can buy and sell USDT person to person on four networks: Ethereum (ERC-20), Tron (TRC-20), Solana (SPL) and BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20). You must pick the network for every trade; see 'Which USDT network should I pick — ERC-20, TRC-20, SPL, or BEP-20?'

USDT is for trading only. You can't pay {brand}'s fees with it: listing fees are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR, and first-message and featured-slot fees in BLURT.

what_is_usdc.a:
USDC (USD Coin) is a stablecoin: a crypto token made to stay worth about 1 US dollar. It is issued by the company Circle.

On {brand} you can buy and sell USDC person to person on four networks: Ethereum (ERC-20), Solana (SPL), Base and Polygon. Pick one that both you and your trading partner use. The order form makes you choose, because coins sent on the wrong network can be lost.

USDC is for trading only: {brand}'s fees are never paid in USDC. For the honest privacy trade-offs, see [the USDC privacy guide](/privacy/usdc).

why_usdt_warning.q: Why does {brand} show a chip about how USDT is issued and transmitted?
why_usdt_warning.a:
{brand} shows this chip to share two facts, so you can choose with open eyes:

• **Tether can freeze addresses.** Tether, the company behind USDT, can freeze the USDT at an address, and has done so.
• **USDT payments are public.** On all four networks (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BNB Smart Chain) anyone can see the transactions. That's how those chains work, not something special about USDT.

This doesn't make USDT bad: it holds a steady dollar value and is easy to trade almost anywhere. If privacy matters most, XMR is the better tool. If you want a coin no company can freeze, look at {coins:btc,blurt,bch,ltc,dash,doge,dcr,sol,eth,xrp|or}. The chip is information, not a verdict.

why_usdc_warning.q: Why does {brand} show a privacy warning when I trade USDC?
why_usdc_warning.a:
For the same reason as USDT: USDC is a stablecoin run by a company. The warning shares two facts:

• **Circle can freeze addresses.** Circle, the company behind USDC, can freeze the USDC at an address on any supported network, and has done so.
• **USDC payments are public** on all four networks (Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon).

The other coins here ({coins:-usdt,-usdc,-dai|list}) have no company that can freeze them.

Many traders accept this trade-off for a steady dollar value, and that's fine. The warning appears on {brand}'s order form and in the window where you share an address; it never blocks anything, it just makes sure the choice is yours. An operator can also switch USDC off for their whole site. If so, pick another coin or another site.

which_usdt_network.q: Which USDT network should I pick — ERC-20, TRC-20, SPL, or BEP-20?
which_usdt_network.a:
Pick a network that you and your trading partner both use. Rough fees, as shown in the order form:

• **Tron (TRC-20):** about $1, fast. The most common for person-to-person trades.
• **Ethereum (ERC-20):** about $5–20, slow. Accepted almost everywhere.
• **Solana (SPL):** under $0.01, fast. Needs a Solana wallet on both sides.
• **BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20):** about $0.30, fast, less common.

There is **no default** on {brand}: the order form won't post a USDT order until you choose. That's on purpose, because USDT sent on the wrong network can be lost for good. Take extra care with Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain: their addresses look the same (both start with `0x`). Before you send, check the network named next to the address in the chat.

which_usdc_network.q: Which USDC network should I use?
which_usdc_network.a:
Pick a network that you and your trading partner both use. Rough fees, as shown in the order form:

• **Solana (SPL):** under $0.01, fast. Needs a Solana wallet on both sides.
• **Base:** about $0.01, fast. Works with Ethereum-style wallets.
• **Polygon:** about $0.01, fast. Also works with Ethereum-style wallets.
• **Ethereum (ERC-20):** about $5–20, slow. Accepted almost everywhere, but costly for small trades.

**Watch out:** Ethereum, Base and Polygon addresses look exactly the same (they all start with `0x`), but each network keeps its own separate balance. If you send USDC on Polygon to an address your partner gave you for Base, it lands on Polygon and their Base wallet won't show it. The order form makes you choose a network, and a shared address in the chat says which network to send on. Always check it before you send.

what_is_dai.a:
DAI is a stablecoin: a coin meant to stay worth about one US dollar. It is run by MakerDAO, not by a single company like Tether (USDT) or Circle (USDC).

• **No freeze button.** The DAI token itself gives nobody a way to freeze your address.
• **Partly backed by USDC.** Some of what keeps DAI at $1 is USDC, which Circle *can* freeze. So DAI is more independent than USDT or USDC, but not fully.
• **Not private.** Every DAI payment is public on its blockchain.

On {brand} you can trade DAI on four networks: Ethereum, Polygon, Base and Arbitrum One. You pick one when you post, and both of you must use that same network (see "Which DAI network should I use?").

You can't pay listing fees in DAI — those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR. More tips: [DAI privacy guide](/privacy/dai).

why_dai_warning.q: Why does {brand} show a privacy warning when I trade DAI?
why_dai_warning.a:
