Because DAI is only partly independent, and never private. The warning says three things:

• **No freeze button on DAI itself.** Unlike USDT and USDC, nobody can block your address on the DAI token. That is a real plus.
• **Some backing is USDC.** Part of what keeps DAI at $1 is USDC, and Circle can freeze USDC. So Circle's power reaches DAI indirectly.
• **Everything is public.** Anyone can see DAI payments on Ethereum, Polygon, Base and Arbitrum.

The warning is just information — it never stops you from trading. A site's operator can also switch DAI off for their whole site.

which_dai_network.q: Which DAI network should I use?
which_dai_network.a:
Use a network you and your trade partner both have. {brand} supports DAI on four:

• **Ethereum (ERC-20)** — works almost everywhere, but fees are high (often $5–20 a payment).
• **Polygon** — low fees, usually cents.
• **Base** — Coinbase's network on top of Ethereum; low fees.
• **Arbitrum One** — another network on top of Ethereum; low fees.

**Be careful:** all four use the same kind of address (`0x…`), so an address looks identical on every one. But each network keeps its own separate balance. DAI sent on the wrong network may be lost, or very hard to get back.

You pick the network when you post the order, and the address you share in chat names it too. Still, agree on the network in chat before anyone sends.

arbitrage_morphit_vs_exchanges.q: How does arbitrage between {brand} and centralized/decentralized exchanges work?
arbitrage_morphit_vs_exchanges.a:
{brand} keeps arbitrage cheap. Posting an order costs only a small listing fee (about 12.5¢ in BLURT, or 25¢ in BTC or XMR). Replying to someone else's order costs no {brand} fee, just Blurt's tiny network fee. And because {brand} never holds your coins, there are no withdrawal fees, limits or waiting times.

If you see a price gap between {brand} and an exchange (Coinbase, Kraken, Uniswap and so on), post an order on the cheap side. Choose **Market price** and add a small +/- percent: the order then follows the market rate, so you never have to re-price it.

How you settle is up to you and your trade partner: wallet to wallet for crypto-for-crypto, or any payment method you both agree on.

One limit: an account with more than 3 orders live (or posted in the last 24 hours) pays a higher BLURT fee for each extra one — 1.25× for the 4th, 1.56× for the 5th, and rising. It is there to stop spam.

market_making.q: Can I market-make or run a trading bot on {brand}?
market_making.a:
Yes. {brand} welcomes market makers and bots.

• **Low cost.** There's no maker or taker fee. Posting an order costs a small listing fee (about 12.5¢ in BLURT, or 25¢ in BTC or XMR); replying to someone else's order costs no {brand} fee.
• **Orders that price themselves.** Choose **Market price** with a +/- percent, and the order follows the market rate on its own.
• **Open data.** Read the orderbook through the public `/v1` API and its live stream, the RSS feeds or the read-only MCP tools — no API key, no signup, no KYC.
• **Your keys, your coins.** An order is a plain Blurt transaction. Your bot signs and sends it itself; {brand} never holds your funds.

One limit: an account with more than 3 orders live (or posted in the last 24 hours) pays a higher BLURT fee for each extra one — 1.25× for the 4th, 1.56× for the 5th, and rising. A bot that keeps many orders open pays that higher rate when it pays in BLURT; the BTC and XMR fee stays the same.

what_is_doge.a:
DOGE is Dogecoin, one of the best-known coins. Like Bitcoin, every payment is public on its blockchain. No company issues it, and nobody can freeze your coins. It is merge-mined with Litecoin, so the same miners help secure both.

On {brand}, DOGE is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** start with `D` (most common), or with `9` or `A` (rare).

**Privacy:** Dogecoin has no privacy features. Use a fresh receive address for every trade — most wallets make one for you. More tips: [DOGE privacy guide](/privacy/doge).

what_is_zec.a:
ZEC is Zcash. With Zcash you choose, per address, whether payments are public or private:

• **Transparent addresses** (`t1…`, `t3…`) work like Bitcoin: anyone can see who paid whom, and how much.
• **Shielded addresses** (`zs1…`, and the newer `u1…`) keep payments private: when both of you use shielded addresses, the sender, the receiver and the amount are hidden.

{brand} accepts all of these. Agree with your trade partner which kind to use — some older wallets can't send to `u1…` addresses.

On {brand}, ZEC is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR). More tips: [ZEC privacy guide](/privacy/zec).

what_is_arrr.q: What is Pirate Chain (ARRR), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_arrr.a:
Pirate Chain (ARRR) is a coin where **every** payment is private: the sender, the receiver and the amount are always hidden. It has no public (transparent) addresses at all. It is on {brand} so people can trade it person to person, without ID.

On {brand}, ARRR is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** start with `zs1` and are 78 characters long. They look exactly like Zcash addresses, so check that the order says ARRR, and receive with a Pirate Chain wallet.

A site's operator can switch ARRR off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [ARRR privacy guide](/privacy/arrr).

what_is_dcr.q: What is Decred (DCR), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_dcr.a:
Decred (DCR) is secured by both miners and coin holders: miners make each block, and holders with staking "tickets" vote on it. Holders also vote on changes to the rules.

Payments are public by default, like Bitcoin. The Decred wallet has optional mixing (CoinShuffle++) for more privacy.

On {brand}, DCR is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** start with `Ds` (most common) or `Dc`, and are 35 characters long. Use a fresh one for each trade.

A site's operator can switch DCR off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [DCR privacy guide](/privacy/dcr).

what_is_sol.q: What is Solana (SOL), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_sol.a:
Solana (SOL) is a fast proof-of-stake blockchain: validators who stake SOL take turns making blocks. Nobody can freeze your coins. Every payment is public.

On {brand}, SOL is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** are 32–44 letters and numbers (most are 44). A SOL address looks just like a USDT or USDC address on Solana, so check that the order says SOL.

**Copy and paste addresses — never type them.** Solana addresses have no built-in typo check, so a mistyped one can be a real address nobody owns, and the coins are lost.

Use a fresh address for each trade. A site's operator can switch SOL off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [SOL privacy guide](/privacy/sol).

what_is_eth.q: What is Ethereum (ETH), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_eth.a:
Ethereum (ETH) is the coin of the Ethereum blockchain, which has run on proof-of-stake since 2022. Nobody can freeze your ETH. Every payment is public.

On {brand}, ETH is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** start with `0x` and are 42 characters long. An ETH address looks exactly like a USDT, USDC or DAI address, so check that the order says ETH. {brand} trades ETH on the main Ethereum network only — not on Base, Arbitrum or Polygon.

**Paste the raw `0x…` address, never type it.** {brand} doesn't accept names like `alice.eth` and doesn't check an address's typo checksum. Also make sure it is a normal wallet address, not a smart contract, which may refuse the ETH.

A site's operator can switch ETH off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [ETH privacy guide](/privacy/eth).

what_is_xrp.q: What is Ripple (XRP), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_xrp.a:
XRP is the coin of the XRP Ledger. There is no mining: a list of trusted validators agrees on each new entry. Nobody can freeze native XRP. Every payment is public.

On {brand}, XRP is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** start with `r` and are 25–35 characters long.

Two things to know before you trade:
• **No destination tags.** {brand} can't pass along a destination tag (the extra number exchanges ask for). So whoever receives the XRP must share their own wallet's address — never an exchange deposit address, or the XRP can land in the exchange's pool and never reach them.
• **1 XRP minimum for a new address.** An XRP address only exists once it holds at least 1 XRP. Sending less to a brand-new address fails, so its first payment must be at least 1 XRP.

A site's operator can switch XRP off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [XRP privacy guide](/privacy/xrp).

what_is_bch.q: What is Bitcoin Cash (BCH), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_bch.a:
Bitcoin Cash (BCH) is a coin that split off from Bitcoin in 2017. Like Bitcoin, every payment is public, and nobody can freeze your coins.

On {brand}, BCH is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses:** {brand} accepts the modern CashAddr format (`bitcoincash:q…` or `bitcoincash:p…`, with or without the `bitcoincash:` part) and the old format starting with `1` or `3`. Old-format BCH addresses look just like Bitcoin addresses, so check that the order says BCH.

Use a fresh address for each trade; CashFusion (optional mixing in some BCH wallets) can add privacy. A site's operator can switch BCH off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [BCH privacy guide](/privacy/bch).

what_is_ltc.q: What is Litecoin (LTC), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_ltc.a:
Litecoin (LTC) is one of the oldest coins, started in 2011 from Bitcoin's code. Like Bitcoin, payments are public and nobody can freeze your coins.

On {brand}, LTC is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses:** {brand} accepts addresses starting with `L`, `M`, `3` or `ltc1`. An LTC address starting with `3` looks like a Bitcoin address, so check that the order says LTC.

**Privacy:** Litecoin has an optional private mode called MWEB, but MWEB addresses (`ltcmweb1…`) can't be shared on {brand} — you receive LTC at a regular address. Use a fresh one for each trade.

A site's operator can switch LTC off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [LTC privacy guide](/privacy/ltc).

what_is_dash.q: What is Dash (DASH), and why is it on {brand}?
what_is_dash.a:
Dash (DASH) is a Bitcoin-style coin: payments are public by default, and nobody can freeze your coins. Dash wallets offer optional mixing called PrivateSend for more privacy.

On {brand}, DASH is **trade-only**: you can buy and sell it, but you can't pay listing fees with it (those are paid in BLURT, BTC or XMR).

**Addresses** start with `X` (most common) or `7`, and are 34 characters long. Use a fresh one for each trade.

A site's operator can switch DASH off for their site; other Morphit sites can still trade it. More tips: [DASH privacy guide](/privacy/dash).

wallet_developer_api.q: I'm a wallet developer — can I integrate Morphit's orderbook into my wallet UI?
wallet_developer_api.a:
Yes, please. Every Morphit site serves the same free, public, read-only API at `/v1/…` — no API key, no signup. It is documented in `docs/API.md` in the source code.

**What you can build:**
• An orderbook screen filtered to the coins your wallet supports (`/v1/orderbook?asset=…`)
• Live updates without polling (`/v1/orderbook/stream`)
• Trader reputation: rating and feedback count (`/v1/accounts/<name>/feedback`); each orderbook entry also carries the trader's rating and completed trades
• Order details: amounts, payment methods, region, terms

**Good to know:**
• Writing doesn't go through the API. Posting an order or a reply is a Blurt transaction your wallet signs with the user's keys.
• Chat is end-to-end encrypted inside the user's app. Most chat routes are deliberately left out of `docs/API.md`; open an issue if you need them.
• The default limit is 120 list requests a minute per IP. Need more? Run your own Morphit node.
• `/v1/instances` lists other Morphit sites. They all read the same Blurt chain, so their orderbooks largely match (an operator can switch some coins off).
• TypeScript types for the responses are in `packages/indexer-client`.
• To import Morphit's 12-word seed phrases, see `docs/SEED-IMPORT-FOR-WALLET-DEVELOPERS.md`.

Morphit's code is AGPL-3.0. Questions? Join `#agorise:matrix.org` or open an issue at git.agorise.net/agorise/morphit.

how_to_spread_morphit.q: How do I get people to use {brand}?
how_to_spread_morphit.a:
Word of mouth. Every person you bring makes the orderbook more useful for everyone. Ideas that cost little or nothing:

• **Write about it** on Blurt.blog, your own blog or Substack, and share it where it's on-topic.
• **Demo it at meetups** — Bitcoin, Monero, privacy, freedom-tech and agorist groups. Five minutes is enough.
• **Print flyers and stickers** with a big QR code to your site and one line, like "Buy crypto, no ID". Try community boards, cafés, libraries, campuses and factory gates at shift change.
• **Reach other coin communities.** Morphit supports Ethereum, Solana, XRP, Pirate Chain, Decred and more — "trade your coin person to person, no KYC" lands well.
• **Operators:** pay a local promoter a small salary plus bonuses in BLURT for new signups, first trades or demos.

**Don't:**
• Spam groups you're not part of — it burns the name.
• Pitch people happy with their exchange. Pitch the unbanked, the privacy-minded and people whose accounts got frozen.
• Overpromise. {brand} has no escrow, no referee and no guaranteed buyers.

Orders posted on one Morphit site show up on the other Morphit sites too, so local growth helps everyone.

totp_2fa_what_is_it.q: What is two-factor authentication and how do I enable it on {brand}?
totp_2fa_what_is_it.a:
Two-factor authentication (2FA) means unlocking your account in {brand} takes two things: your password, plus a 6-digit code from an app on your phone. The code changes every 30 seconds and can't be used twice while the page is open.

It's optional. {brand} will never force it on you or nag you about it.

To turn it on, go to Settings → Two-factor authentication (2FA) → **Set up 2FA**. Install an open-source authenticator app (we suggest Aegis, 2FAS or Ente Auth), scan the QR code, type the code the app shows, and save your 10 backup codes somewhere safe. The option is there when your account is saved on this device with a password.

Honest limits: 2FA is a lock inside the app, not extra encryption. It stops someone who learned your password from unlocking your account in {brand}. But the 2FA secret sits in the same encrypted file as your keys, so someone with that file AND your password could open it with other software. For a factor that is never in that file, use a YubiKey in YubiKey-only mode (Settings → Hardware key).

totp_2fa_lost_authenticator.q: I lost my authenticator app — how do I get back in?
totp_2fa_lost_authenticator.a:
Use a backup code. When you set up 2FA, {brand} gave you 10 backup codes (they look like `XXXX-XXXX`). On the unlock screen, type one where it asks for the 6-digit code — the box takes either. Each backup code works once; {brand} marks it used.

No backup codes left? Sign in again with your 12-word seed phrase: on the unlock screen choose **Sign in with seed phrase**, type the 12 words and choose a new password. Your keys come from the seed, so you get everything back. 2FA is off after that; you can set it up again. (If you joined with an existing Blurt account, you have no seed — use the **Blurt posting key** option instead.)

Nobody can reset 2FA for you. {brand} never holds your keys, so if you lose the authenticator, the backup codes AND the seed, the account can't be recovered.

totp_2fa_why_not_google_authenticator.a:
Two reasons:

• **Closed source.** Nobody outside Google can check what it does with your 2FA secrets.
• **Cloud sync.** It backs up your 2FA secrets to your Google account by default (you have to opt out), and they aren't end-to-end encrypted with a password only you know. Anyone who takes over your Google account could get all your codes at once — which defeats the point of a *second*, separate factor.

{brand} suggests open-source apps where you decide where backups go: **Aegis** (Android, encrypted local backups), **2FAS** (iOS and Android, cloud backup only if you turn it on) or **Ente Auth** (every platform, end-to-end encrypted sync).

Already use another authenticator you trust, such as KeePassXC or Bitwarden Authenticator? That's fine. Our list is a suggestion for new users, not a ban.

privacy_coins_onchain.q: How does {brand} keep my privacy-coin trades private?
privacy_coins_onchain.a:
{brand} trades several privacy coins — {coins:xmr,zec,arrr,dash,dcr} — and protects them all the same way.

**Your coins never touch {brand}'s chain.** You send them straight from your wallet to your trade partner's, on that coin's own network. The Blurt chain {brand} uses carries only the public listing, your encrypted chat, any listing fee paid in BLURT and, if you leave one, your public review.

**What a listing shows.** A listing is an ad, so its side (buy or sell), coin, currency, price, amount range, payment methods, region (if you set one) and terms are public — that's how people find it. Nothing extra is added: the listing's ID is a random code (`order-…`) that doesn't name the coin, the expiry is rounded down to the day, and no IP address, time zone or browser details are attached. It does carry the language you choose and the tag of the site you post from.

**Amount jitter.** When you share a receive amount in chat, {brand} adds a tiny random amount so the payment can't be matched to your listing by its size. It's on by default.

**Listing fees.** You pay in BLURT (the default), or in BTC or XMR where the site accepts them — never in ZEC, ARRR, DASH or DCR, so their transaction IDs never appear on the Blurt chain. If you pay in XMR, that fee payment's transaction ID and key are written into your listing. Want no Monero link at all? Pay in BLURT; at the base rate it is also half the price.

Each coin has its own [privacy guide](/privacy) — for example [Monero](/privacy/xmr).

what_is_barter.a:
Barter lets you buy or sell goods and services — baskets, bike repairs, a crate of oranges — and settle in crypto.

**How it works:**
• Describe exactly what you're offering in the Terms (required).
• Set its value in your local currency — one price or a range.
• Tick the crypto(s) you'll accept, say XMR, BTC and DOGE. It's **one listing**, not one per coin.

When you and the buyer settle up in chat, {brand} only lets you share a payment address or report a payment in the coins the listing accepts.

**Goods change hands outside {brand}** — in person or by post — and {brand} never touches the goods or the payment. Meet in a public place, share only what you need to, and treat a stranger like a stranger.

Barter is for trading wares only: you can't use it to pay {brand}'s listing fee.

what_is_a_txid.q: What is a Transaction ID (or Hash)?
what_is_a_txid.a:
When you send crypto, the blockchain gives that payment a unique ID called the Transaction ID. Wallets name it differently: “TxID”, “Transaction Hash”, “Tx Hash” or just “Hash” (Mycelium, for example, calls it “Hash”). It's a long string of letters and numbers, usually 64 characters (Blurt's are 40).

To find it: open your wallet, tap the payment you sent, and copy the ID or Hash it shows.

Pasting it into {brand} lets your trade partner — or, for a listing fee, {brand} — check that the payment really happened.

Anyone with the ID can look the payment up on a public block explorer. On open chains like Bitcoin that shows the amounts and addresses involved; on Monero it shows very little.

ip_address_and_rpc_nodes.q: Does anything see or leak my IP address when I use {brand}?
ip_address_and_rpc_nodes.a:
**What this site sees.** Like any website, the server gets your IP address with each request. The code keeps it only in memory, for rate limits — about a minute for ordinary requests, up to 24 hours for the signup limits — and never writes it to disk or a log, or sends it anywhere. The web server keeps addresses only in memory for its own limits and short bans, and keeps no access log with them. No cookies, analytics, trackers or telemetry. Orders, encrypted chat, balances and the block explorer data are all secured on-chain.

**The one possible IP leak.** At most once a day (and once after each site update, or when you press **Try again** on a fee panel), your browser asks a public network node — a Blurt RPC node run by someone else — for the signed release record that says which Morphit version is current. That is two small requests to one node (each may come with a CORS preflight): the last 100 entries of @morphit's history, then the block holding the release. Only if that node fails, sends a record that can't be verified, or names a different release than this site runs, is another node asked the same. If the release is older than those 100 entries, one more history request is made (up to about 115 KB). The result is remembered for 24 hours and shared by all your tabs; if a node offers only a release older than this site's, your browser asks again within the hour. If your browser blocks this site's storage, it can't remember, so it asks each time you open {brand}. You can watch all of it in your browser's Network tab.

**Which nodes.** On an https or plain-http clearnet address: the five public clearnet nodes. On a .onion address: only the seven .onion nodes. On an .i2p address: only the seven .b32.i2p nodes.

**Why.** The record names the current release, Morphit's fee addresses and the fingerprints of the app's start-up files, and it must carry @morphit's signature. A bad node can make the check fail or delay an update notice, but can't fake a release. It catches an outdated or damaged build — not an operator who deliberately serves altered code, since that operator also serves the check.

**What a node learns.** Your IP address, this site's address (on .onion or .i2p, that hidden address), your browser's User-Agent and language, and that someone asked for @morphit's release history. Not your username, orders, chat or balances.

**Use Tor or a VPN** and this is closed: both hide your IP from the nodes and from your operator.

active_key.title: Active key
active_key.body: One of the three private keys your {brand} account has. The active key is for moving BLURT — paying listing fees, sending tips, transferring balances. {brand} asks for it (or rather, for the password that unlocks it on your device) only when you're about to spend. It never leaves your browser.

blockchain.title: Blockchain
blockchain.body: A blockchain is a shared record book that thousands of independent computers each keep a full copy of — instead of one company keeping it on a single server. Once something is written in, no single party can quietly erase or rewrite it, because every copy would have to agree to the change. {brand} settles on a blockchain (called Blurt) so your orders, ratings, and messages live somewhere no operator — and no government — can secretly alter or take down. That's what makes Morphit hard to censor or shut off: there's no central database for anyone to seize.

blurt.title: Blurt (BLURT)
blurt.body: Blurt is two things: a blockchain (where Morphit's order ops, fees, and chat ciphertext live), and its coin, BLURT, which you pay listing fees with. The coin and the chain share the same name. There is no Morphit token — Morphit uses BLURT directly.

blurt_power.title: Blurt Power (BP)
blurt_power.body: BLURT that you have "powered up" — staked into your account so it can't be spent immediately and it earns you a passive income from staking your BLURT coins. BP gives you weight when voting on Blurt content (separate from {brand}) and is the basis for delegation. {brand} doesn't require any BP; its welcome and loyalty rewards are BP lent to you, which adds to your voting weight.

broadcast.title: Broadcast
broadcast.body: To send a signed operation to the blockchain. Posting an order, cancelling an order, leaving feedback, sending an encrypted chat message — all of these are broadcasts. Once a broadcast lands in a block, it can't be undone (the operation is on-chain forever); only superseded by a later one.

counterparty.title: Counterparty
counterparty.body: The other person in a trade. If you posted a sell order and someone messages you to buy, that person is your counterparty. The word is neutral — it doesn't mean "opponent." Both sides of every {brand} trade have a counterparty: each is the other's.

custom_json.title: custom_json
custom_json.body: A type of operation on the blockchain that carries arbitrary structured data. Morphit's order ops, feedback ops, chat envelopes, and operator registrations are all custom_json operations — they ride on the chain's existing infrastructure rather than requiring a new chain. You don't need to interact with custom_json directly; {brand} builds them for you.

delegation.title: Delegation
delegation.body: Lending some of your BP to another account temporarily, without giving them control of your underlying BLURT. {brand} doesn't require delegation to use, but operators sometimes delegate to new accounts to give them initial weight. Delegations can be undone (with a cooldown period before the BP becomes liquid again).

federation.title: Federation
federation.body: Multiple independent Morphit instances that share the same orderbook and chat ecosystem because they all read from the same underlying blockchain. If one operator goes offline (or hostile), users move to another and find the same orders, the same trades, the same reputations. Federation is what makes Morphit uncensorable.

feedback.title: Feedback
feedback.body: A signed, on-chain rating you leave for a counterparty after a trade. Feedback is permanent — it can't be deleted, only responded to. Your reputation on {brand} is the sum of feedback others have left for you over time. Both sides of every completed trade are entitled to leave one piece of feedback.

fiat.title: Fiat
fiat.body: Government-issued currency: dollars, euros, yen, pesos, rubles. The opposite of crypto. On {brand}, fiat is what changes hands off-platform — you and your counterparty agree on a price in fiat (e.g. USD), settle the fiat side privately (cash, bank transfer, your choice), and {brand} handles only the crypto side.

indexer.title: Indexer
indexer.body: The component of a Morphit instance that watches the chain, decodes Morphit-relevant operations (orders, feedback, chat envelopes), and serves them to the web frontend in a usable shape. The chain is the source of truth; the indexer is just a fast cache. Run by the operator, not by you.

instance.title: Instance
instance.body: A single Morphit website, run by one operator — the site you're on right now is one instance. Because Morphit is federated, many independent instances all read the same blockchain and show the same orders, trades, and reputations. If one instance blocks you or goes offline, you can switch to any other instance and pick up exactly where you left off.

listing_fee.title: Listing fee
listing_fee.body: The small BLURT fee {brand} charges when you post a new order. The fee covers operator costs and disincentivizes spam orderbooks. The first order from a new account is free. Listing fees scale gently with how often you post. Cancelling an order does NOT refund the listing fee — it's the cost of the listing, not the trade.

network_fee.title: Network fee
network_fee.body: Two unrelated things share this name in casual speech: (1) {brand}'s listing fee — the BLURT cost of posting an order; and (2) the Bitcoin or Monero on-chain fee that miners take when you settle the crypto side of a trade. {brand} only ever charges the first; the second is between you and the underlying network when you make the actual transfer.

operator.title: Operator
operator.body: The person or team running a particular Morphit instance — the website you're looking at right now is operated by someone. The operator runs the indexer and relay servers, sets policies for their instance (rate limits, fee tiers, kill-switch), and earns a share of the listing fees that flow through. If an operator goes hostile, you can switch to a different instance and find your same orders, same trades, same reputation.

password.title: Password
password.body: What unlocks your private keys on your device. {brand} never sees, sends, stores, or knows your password — it's used locally by your browser to decrypt the encrypted bundle of keys held in your browser's storage. If you forget your password, the keys are gone; that's why {brand} asks you to write down your seed phrase during onboarding.

permlink.title: Permlink
permlink.body: The unique short identifier of an order on the blockchain — something like `morphit-o-2k4f9`. Permlinks let you (and the chain, and other Morphit instances) refer to a specific order without ambiguity. The order's URL on any Morphit instance ends in its permlink, so order links are portable across instances.

posting_key.title: Posting key
posting_key.body: Another of your account's three private keys. The posting key is for signing content — chat messages, feedback, comments. It's lower-trust than the active key (it can't move BLURT) so a compromise is less catastrophic. {brand} uses it for chat-payload signing and feedback ops; you'll never need to handle it directly.

relay.title: Relay
relay.body: The component of a Morphit instance that handles things the indexer can't — chat envelope acceptance, fee verification, kill-switch enforcement, anti-spam policies. The relay is the moving-parts side of an instance (the indexer is read-only against the chain). Run by the operator, not by you.

release_op.title: Release op
release_op.body: An on-chain operation signed by the @morphit account that announces a new Morphit release: its version, the SHA-256 of its source tarball, and the hashes of the files that start the website. At most once a day your browser reads the newest one from a public Blurt node (a second node only if the first fails) and checks its signature; when the site runs that version, it compares the files it loaded with the signed hashes and warns you if they differ. That catches a file changed by accident or by a partly compromised server — not a hostile operator, who serves the checking code too.

seed_phrase.title: Seed phrase
seed_phrase.body: Twelve English words that, taken together, are the master backup of your account. From the seed phrase your device can re-derive every key your account has. If your device dies and you lose your password, the seed phrase is what gets you back in. Write it down on paper. Don't take a screenshot. Don't email it to yourself. Don't store it in a password manager that lives on the same device.

sign.title: Sign
sign.body: To attach a cryptographic signature to a piece of data using one of your private keys, proving the data came from you and hasn't been altered. When {brand} asks you to "unlock to sign," it's about to ask the chain to accept an action on your behalf — posting an order, sending a message, paying a fee. The signing happens locally on your device; the private key never leaves.

glossary.heading: Glossary
glossary.intro: Plain-language explanations of the words {brand} uses. If a term in the UI is confusing, it should be defined here. If it isn't, please file an issue report.
glossary.footnote: These definitions are deliberately short. For longer or more technical answers, see the {faqOpen}FAQ{faqClose}.

aead.title: AEAD
aead.body: Authenticated encryption: it both encrypts the message and detects any tampering, in a single step.

dns.title: DNS
dns.body: Domain Name System: the internet's directory that turns a name like morphit.io into a server address.

ecdh.title: ECDH
ecdh.body: Elliptic-Curve Diffie–Hellman: a method for two parties to derive a shared secret without ever sending it.

ecies.title: ECIES
ecies.body: A standard scheme for encrypting a message to someone's public key, so only the holder of the matching private key can read it.

ens.title: ENS
ens.body: Ethereum Name Service: maps readable names like yourbrand.eth to decentralized website content.

ipfs.title: IPFS
ipfs.body: InterPlanetary File System: a peer-to-peer network that serves files by their content hash instead of a server address.

mcp.title: MCP
mcp.body: Model Context Protocol: an open standard that lets AI assistants read data through well-defined tools.

morphit.title: Morphit
morphit.body: Morphit is the open source software that runs this website and many others like it, each one an instance run by its own operator. It was developed by the Dev Team at Agorise. Every instance reads the same orders, reputations and encrypted chats from the Blurt blockchain, so your account works on all of them. The code is public for anyone to check, and it never holds your coins or your keys.

p2p.title: P2P
p2p.body: Peer-to-peer: participants connect and transact directly, with no central server or middleman.

pwa.title: PWA
pwa.body: Progressive Web App: a website you can install and use like a native app, even offline.

rss.title: RSS
rss.body: A standard web-feed format for subscribing to a site's updates — here, {brand}'s live order feed.

tls.title: TLS
tls.body: Transport Layer Security: the encryption that protects data in transit — the 'S' in HTTPS.

x25519.title: X25519
x25519.body: A fast, modern elliptic curve used for key agreement: two sides compute a shared secret from each other's public keys.

home.hero_title: Anonymously trade cryptocurrencies, fiat, goods, services and more
home.hero_body: {brand} connects buyers and sellers directly. No KYC, non-custodial, no cookies, E2EE, no tracking, no escrow, private by default, open source, fully-distributed

privacy.title: Privacy first
privacy.body: No KYC, email, phone/SMS, cookies, analytics or selfies. Pick a cool username, that's it, seriously.

true_p2p.title: True P2P
true_p2p.body: Assets move directly between Buyer and Seller only. No exchange wallet, escrow, arbitrators or middleman.

unstoppable.title: Unstoppable by design
unstoppable.body: Reachable on clearnet, Tor, Lokinet, I2P, ENS and Federated instance runners. Block one and many others remain.

discoverability.title: Discoverability
discoverability.body: Federation uses an open public blockchain and RSS for orderbook distribution, trade finalization and user reputation.

encrypted_chat.title: Encrypted Chat
encrypted_chat.body: Buyer/Seller conversations are 100% private, E2EE and immutable for posterity in case you have a future dispute.

reputation.title: Reputation is everything
reputation.body: Use any number of different websites and your good reputation follows you. Your personal trades are always there.

trade_anything.title: Trade anything
trade_anything.body: 16+ cryptos plus direct goods, services and even barter. Cross-asset, cross-network, cross-medium.

instances.title: Known Morphit instances
instances.intro: Morphit is federated. Independent Operators run Morphit instances, and they get paid 90% of all of the BLURT listing fees on their sites. The more people that use their site, the more they get paid. Learn more about it in the [FAQ], or [download] Morphit to your server now to [run your own node].
instances.bookmark_tip: 💡 Tip: bookmark a few of these instances — and their Tor, I2P, Lokinet or ENS addresses. The orderbook lives on the public blockchain. So if any one site is ever inaccessible, you can reach the very same orders and trades in many other places.

onboarding.title: Let's set up your keys

plan.heading: What we're building
plan.subtitle: The plan is public. We ship in phases so every piece is done well.
plan.phase_1_body: The shell, the ten languages, the keygen flow, the searchable help — everything a first-time visitor needs, without any server-side account.
plan.phase_2_body: Connect to the chain. Ship the relay service that broadcasts user-signed operations. Release-discovery pointer lands on-chain.
plan.phase_3_body: Indexer goes live. Browse, filter, and post orders. 15-minute replace window. Sybil-resistant fee escalation. Self-trade detection.
plan.phase_4_body: End-to-end encrypted chat. Signed feedback with buyer/seller roles. Public reputation profiles.
plan.phase_5_body: Live BTC / XMR / BLURT payment flows. Tor, Lokinet, and I2P hidden services. IPFS release mirror. PWA + Federated instances onboarding.
plan.phase_6_body: Developers can embed a scoped orderbook screen into their UI. Users can search/browse/respond to offers without leaving the UI they trust.
plan.phase_7_body: We have not started this phase yet. As more coins are requested, each one will be reviewed. Some coins might shut down, so they will be removed. The world is entering a new monetary system, so staying ahead of it is imperative.

asset_explainer.btc: Bitcoin (BTC) — the original cryptocurrency, used worldwide. Public ledger; transactions are visible. Network fees and confirmation time vary with network demand.
asset_explainer.xmr: Monero (XMR) — privacy-first cryptocurrency. Hides amounts, balances, senders and recipients by default. Ideal if privacy matters to you.
asset_explainer.blurt: BLURT — the coin of Blurt, the social blockchain {brand} runs on. Fast (3-second blocks), zero-fee transfers, built-in rewards system. Perfect for reputation-building, trade posterity and connecting with like-minded people.
asset_explainer.usdt: Tether (USDT) — a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to USD. Centrally controlled — Tether Inc. can freeze any address.
asset_explainer.bch: Bitcoin Cash (BCH). Forked from Bitcoin in 2017 to favor bigger blocks and lower per-transaction fees over fee-market dynamics. Transparent ledger like BTC; no issuer can freeze addresses. Trade-only on {brand} — listing fees still paid in BLURT, BTC, or XMR.
asset_explainer.ltc: Litecoin (LTC). Forked from Bitcoin in 2011 with faster 2.5-minute blocks and Scrypt mining. Transparent like Bitcoin — every transaction is publicly visible on the chain. No central issuer; nobody can freeze your addresses.
asset_explainer.dash: Dash (DASH). Forked from Litecoin in 2014 with masternode-coordinated services. Transparent at the base layer like Bitcoin — every transaction is publicly visible on the chain. No central issuer; nobody can freeze your addresses. Optional PrivateSend mixing (a CoinJoin variant coordinated by masternodes) provides opt-in privacy.
asset_explainer.usdc: USD Coin (USDC) — a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to USD, issued by Circle. Centrally controlled — Circle can freeze any address.
asset_explainer.dai: DAI is a USD-pegged stablecoin by MakerDAO. More decentralized than USDT/USDC at the contract level (no admin freeze) but partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module.
asset_explainer.doge: Dogecoin (DOGE). Launched 2013 as a fair-launch fork of Lucky Coin (itself a Litecoin fork). Transparent at the base layer like Bitcoin — every transaction is publicly visible on the chain. No central issuer; nobody can freeze your addresses. Merge-mined with Litecoin since 2014 (auxiliary proof-of-work).
asset_explainer.zec: Zcash (ZEC). Launched 2016 as the first practical deployment of zero-knowledge proofs in a cryptocurrency. Transparent and shielded address types coexist on the same chain — t1/t3 addresses are publicly visible like Bitcoin's legacy addresses, while zs1 (Sapling) and u1 (Unified Address with Orchard receivers) use zk-SNARKs to hide sender, recipient, and amount. Choose the address type that matches your trade's privacy posture.
asset_explainer.arrr: Pirate Chain (ARRR) — chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool; every transfer is private by construction. Single address format (zs1 Sapling, bech32, 78 chars). Trade-only on {brand}; listing fees stay BLURT/BTC/XMR.
asset_explainer.dcr: Decred (DCR). A coin whose community votes on how the project is run. Its public ledger is visible like Bitcoin's, and its wallet has an optional privacy mode. No central issuer — nobody can freeze your coins.
asset_explainer.sol: Solana (SOL) — high-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency. Native SOL transfer (not wrapped SOL or SPL tokens). 32-44 character base58 addresses (same shape as USDT-Solana and USDC-Solana addresses; asset field disambiguates).
asset_explainer.eth: Ethereum (ETH) — Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency. Native ETH transfer (not wrapped ETH or ERC-20 tokens). 42-character 0x-prefixed hex addresses (same shape as USDT-ERC20, USDC-ERC20, DAI-ERC20, and every EVM token-account address; asset field + network field disambiguate).
asset_explainer.xrp: Ripple (XRP) — Federated Byzantine Agreement cryptocurrency on the XRP Ledger. 24-34 character base58 addresses starting with `r`. Destination tags (32-bit integers) are required when sending to exchange-hosted addresses — your peer-to-peer counterparty typically does not need one. XRPL accounts need ≥1 XRP base reserve to exist.
asset_explainer.barter: Barter (goods/services). Not a cryptocurrency — you offer wares or a service and get paid in the crypto(s) you choose to accept. Price it in your local currency; you and the buyer work out the details in chat and settle in one of your accepted cryptos. Describe exactly what you're offering in the Terms field.

form.waiver_fiat_hint: 💡 Most BLURT trades on {brand} happen with active Blurt social-network users, existing operators, or via barter. So, pick the fiat denomination that you use locally (USD, EUR, MXN, etc), and offer In-Person or Barter (goods/services) payment methods on Step 3 if you want to offer something else of value.

privacy.index_intro: Most assets traded on {brand} ({coins:btc,bch,ltc,dash,doge,dcr,sol,eth,xrp,blurt,usdt,usdc,dai|list}) live on transparent chains — any observer can read the chain history. Zcash (ZEC) is transparent unless you use its shielded addresses; Pirate Chain (ARRR), like Monero, hides sender, receiver and amount by default. There are concrete steps you can take to make YOUR trades much harder to link, profile, or surveil. This is registry-driven: the next asset we add will get a guide automatically. Beyond individual trades, Morphit also protects privacy at the network level: it can be reached and run entirely over Tor and I2P — a node can even operate with zero clearnet at all — as detailed on the Security page and the instance directory.
privacy.section_fresh_addresses: Use a fresh address every trade
privacy.section_opt_in_tech_intro: Standards that wallets in this ecosystem may implement. {brand} does NOT recommend specific wallet software — even reputable wallets have been compromised. Search for a wallet that supports these standards and review its trust posture yourself.
privacy.no_wallet_recommendation: {brand} does NOT recommend specific wallet software. Even reputable wallets have been compromised or have had hidden flaws. The privacy techniques here are protocol standards, not endorsements — your wallet, your responsibility.

fresh_address_advice.subaddress: This chain supports stealth/subaddress technology natively. Your wallet derives a fresh receive address (subaddress) per trade from your view key. The recipient sees a unique address every time; chain observers cannot link multiple trades to the same wallet.
fresh_address_advice.hd-derived: This chain uses transparent addresses with no native stealth. The standard practice: use a Hierarchical Deterministic (BIP-32) wallet that derives a new receive address per request. Most modern wallets do this automatically. The cost of address reuse is severe — every trade you accept at the same address builds a public record of your activity.
fresh_address_advice.account-reuse: This chain is account-based — your account name is your address. Fresh-account-per-trade is not practical (each new account costs chain resources). Accept that this asset has the highest amount-correlation risk on {brand}. For high-value trades, consider using an alt-account dedicated to that trade.

mweb.name: MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks)
mweb.explain: A native Litecoin protocol-level privacy feature. MWEB hides transaction amounts and breaks the address-to-amount link for transfers that opt in. Per-transaction; not chain-wide. Look for wallets that surface "MWEB" or "Extension Blocks" as an option when sending.

cashfusion.name: CashFusion
cashfusion.explain: A Bitcoin Cash CoinJoin variant designed by the BCH community. Mixes inputs and outputs of varying amounts to defeat both common-input-ownership and amount-correlation heuristics. Run from a wallet that supports CashFusion before or after a trade to launder the on-chain history.

coinjoin.name: CoinJoin
coinjoin.explain: A family of protocols where multiple participants pool inputs and outputs into a single transaction, breaking the common-input-ownership heuristic that links coins to one owner. Multiple implementations exist with different trust models — choose carefully and read the implementation's threat model.

payjoin.name: PayJoin (BIP-78)
payjoin.explain: A two-party cooperative transaction protocol. Sender and receiver both contribute inputs, so chain observers cannot apply the standard "all inputs come from the same wallet" heuristic. {brand}'s address-share modal includes an optional PayJoin endpoint field — if both wallets support BIP-78, the trade automatically uses PayJoin.

privatesend.name: PrivateSend
privatesend.explain: Dash's native CoinJoin variant. Uses denominated input/output amounts and masternode coordination to mix coins among multiple participants, breaking the link between sender and receiver on-chain. Run multiple mixing rounds (more rounds = larger anonymity set = higher fee). Pre-mix in your Dash wallet BEFORE sharing the address — by the time the funds reach {brand} they're already mixed.

shielded-pools.name: Shielded pools (Sapling + Orchard)
shielded-pools.explain: Zcash's protocol-level privacy. Shielded transactions (zs1 Sapling, u1 Unified Address) use zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) to hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Sapling is the established shielded pool (since 2018); Orchard is the newer pool (Network Upgrade 5, 2022) accessed through Unified Addresses. Per-address — recipients pick z/u-addr for shielded transactions or t-addr for transparent. Both transparent and shielded are first-class on the protocol. Wallets that fully support shielded sends: Zashi (mobile, official from Electric Coin Co, Sapling + Orchard), Zecwallet (desktop, Sapling), Nighthawk Wallet (mobile, Sapling). Older wallets may only support transparent (t-addr) sends, so confirm your counterparty's wallet supports the address type you intend to use.

csppmix.name: CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) mixing
csppmix.explain: A wallet-side mixing protocol that bundles your transaction inputs with other participants in a single multi-party round.  After mixing, your outputs are no longer linkable to your original inputs on chain.  Integrated into dcrwallet for Decred — enable the "Mix Account" option.  Opt-in (you choose when to mix); off-protocol (mixing rounds aren't enforced by consensus).

common_practices.fresh_per_trade: **Use a fresh receive address for every trade.** Your wallet should support this; if it doesn't, look for one that does. Address reuse is the single biggest leak.
common_practices.coin_control: **Practice coin control when spending.** When sending coins later, avoid combining the trade output with coins from another source — that combines their address histories permanently.
common_practices.network_layer: **Broadcast through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode.** Your home IP address sees the transaction first; nodes near your IP can correlate it to you. A Tor-aware wallet broadcasts through Tor by default.
common_practices.kyc_touchpoints: **Avoid sending trade coins to or from KYC exchanges.** Once trade coins touch a KYC exchange, the trade becomes legally identifiable by combining exchange records with chain data. If you need to bridge to fiat, route through a self-custodied intermediate step.

what_not_to_do.reuse_address: Do not paste your same receive address into multiple trades.
what_not_to_do.exact_amount: Do not send the exact amount listed on the order — {brand}'s amount-randomizer toggle (the "🔐 Randomize amount" checkbox in the address-share modal) breaks this; leave it ON.
what_not_to_do.combine_utxos: Do not combine the trade output with coins from a different source when you later spend it.
what_not_to_do.clearnet_broadcast: Do not broadcast from your home IP via a non-private wallet — use Tor.

btc.one_line: Transparent chain, fully decentralized — opt-in mixing protocols available.
btc.intro: Bitcoin is the most-analyzed chain in the world. Every transaction is public; every address can be tracked over time. The privacy practices below dramatically reduce how easily a third party can profile your trades — without requiring you to leave BTC.
btc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, PayJoin, CoinJoin, and what to avoid.

xmr.one_line: Privacy by default — stealth addresses, hidden amounts, ring signatures.
xmr.intro: Monero's chain-level privacy hides sender, recipient, and amount by default. By default, your address, amount, and counterparty are hidden from third parties. The practices below are minor tightenings; the chain itself does the heavy lifting.
xmr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Monero trades on {brand}: subaddresses and amount handling.

blurt.one_line: Coordination chain — transparent and account-based. Lowest privacy on {brand}.
blurt.intro: Blurt is {brand}'s coordination chain — orders, chat ciphertexts, fees, and reputation all live here. The chain is fully public and account-based, meaning every BLURT transfer involving your account is permanently visible to anyone. There is no opt-in privacy technology on Blurt.
blurt.caveats: BLURT is structurally the least private asset on {brand}. Your account name is your address; you cannot rotate it. For trades where on-chain privacy matters more than speed and cost, prefer XMR, BTC (with PayJoin), BCH (with CashFusion), LTC (with MWEB), or DASH (with PrivateSend).
blurt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for BLURT trades on {brand}: account-based chain, transparent by design.

usdt.one_line: Centralized — Tether can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdt.intro: USDT's privacy issue is structurally different from the other transparent assets: it's centralized. Tether Inc. can freeze any USDT address on any host chain, and they have used this ability in the past. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Tether's freeze capability.
usdt.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDT remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDT host chains (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BSC) is the same as on any transparent EVM/UTXO/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem (Tornado Cash on ETH, etc.), which we do not endorse or describe further here.
usdt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDT trades on {brand}: centralization risk and host-chain transparency.

bch.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — CashFusion provides opt-in mixing.
bch.intro: Bitcoin Cash shares Bitcoin's transparency model: every transaction visible on chain, every address linkable. CashFusion (a BCH-community CoinJoin variant with amount-randomization) is the main opt-in privacy technology and is well-integrated into several BCH wallets.
bch.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin Cash trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, CashFusion, and what to avoid.

ltc.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — MWEB provides opt-in chain-level privacy.
ltc.intro: Litecoin shares Bitcoin's transparency at the base layer, but adds MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks) — a chain-level opt-in privacy feature that hides amounts and breaks address linkability for transfers that opt in. This is the closest a Bitcoin-family chain comes to native privacy.
ltc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Litecoin trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, MWEB, and what to avoid.

dash.one_line: Transparent base layer, decentralized — PrivateSend provides masternode-coordinated opt-in mixing.
dash.intro: Dash forked from Litecoin in 2014 and shares the same transparent base layer — every address balance and transaction is publicly visible. The chain is fully decentralized; no issuer can freeze addresses. Dash adds PrivateSend, a CoinJoin variant coordinated by the masternode network, providing opt-in mixing at the wallet level. Pre-mixing several rounds before sharing your receiving address is the strongest privacy practice on Dash.
dash.meta_description: Privacy practices for Dash trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, PrivateSend pre-mixing, and what to avoid.
dash.caveats: PrivateSend's anonymity set depends on simultaneous mixing participants. Off-peak hours = smaller set = weaker unlinkability. Masternode coordination is a trust trade-off: the protocol is non-custodial (masternodes never hold your coins) but the coordinator sees the mixing pattern.

usdc.one_line: Centralized — Circle can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdc.intro: USDC's privacy posture mirrors USDT's: it's centralized. Circle (USDC's issuer) can freeze any USDC address on any host chain, and has done so on regulatory request. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Circle's freeze capability. The amount-correlation defense (jitter) IS active for USDC trades — see /{lang}/faq#monero_amount_jitter — but jitter addresses a different threat than centralization.
usdc.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDC remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDC host chains (Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon) is the same as on any transparent EVM/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem, which we do not endorse or describe further here. BEP-20 USDC on BNB Chain is intentionally NOT supported: that variant is Binance-Peg (Binance-custodied wrapper of Circle-issued USDC), adding a second custodian to the existing one.
usdc.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDC trades on {brand}: centralization risk, host-chain transparency, and the amount-jitter defense.

dai.one_line: DAI — USD-pegged stablecoin governed by MakerDAO. No admin freeze on the token, but partly backed by USDC.
dai.meta_description: Honest privacy notes for trading DAI on {brand}: more decentralized than USDT/USDC at the contract level, partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module.
dai.intro: DAI is MakerDAO's USD-pegged stablecoin, deployed on Ethereum and several other EVM chains. It's the most-decentralized US-dollar-pegged asset {brand} supports — but "decentralized" doesn't mean "freeze-immune" or "fully crypto-backed" anymore. This page is the honest picture so you can choose with eyes open.

doge.one_line: Transparent base layer, decentralized via PoW, no native privacy upgrade.
doge.intro: Dogecoin launched in 2013 as a fair-launched fork of an earlier Litecoin variant. Like Bitcoin, every address balance and transaction is publicly visible on the chain. The chain is fully decentralized; no issuer or foundation can freeze addresses. Since 2014 it has been merge-mined with Litecoin (auxiliary proof-of-work), inheriting Litecoin's hashrate security without competing for it.
doge.meta_description: Privacy practices for Dogecoin trades on {brand}: fresh addresses, avoiding chain heuristics, and what tradeoffs to expect.
doge.caveats: Dogecoin has no native privacy upgrade — no PrivateSend equivalent, no confidential transactions, no segwit-enabled mixing. Every receive address you publish on {brand} can be linked to its on-chain history forever. Use a fresh HD-derived address for every trade (your wallet usually does this automatically).

zec.one_line: Transparent and shielded address types coexist; recipients pick per address.
zec.intro: Zcash launched in 2016 as the first deployment of zk-SNARK-based shielded transactions in a cryptocurrency. The chain supports two address families: transparent (t1/t3) which behave like Bitcoin's legacy addresses with publicly visible amounts, and shielded (zs1 Sapling, u1 Unified Address bundling Orchard receivers) which use zero-knowledge proofs to hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Per-trade, the recipient picks the address type that matches their preferred posture. Both are first-class on the protocol.
zec.meta_description: Privacy practices for Zcash trades on {brand}: choosing between transparent and shielded addresses (t-addr, z-addr, u-addr), wallet recommendations, and what each privacy pool does.
zec.caveats: Shielded-to-shielded transactions hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Mixed transactions (shielded-to-transparent or transparent-to-shielded) reveal one side. Transparent-to-transparent reveals both. If your goal is to minimize linkability, use a shielded address (zs1 or u1) and ask the counterparty to send from a shielded address. Wallet support varies: Zashi (mobile, official from Electric Coin Co, Sapling + Orchard), Zecwallet (desktop, Sapling), Nighthawk (mobile, Sapling) — not every wallet supports every address type, so verify your counterparty's wallet handles the address type you publish before sharing it.

arrr.one_line: Chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool; every transfer hides sender, recipient, and amount by construction.
arrr.intro:
Pirate Chain (ARRR) launched in 2018 as a fork of the Zcash codebase, configured so that the Sapling shielded pool is the only available transaction type.  Every transfer goes through zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) that hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain.  Pirate Chain sunsetted the transparent pool early in the chain's life and forcibly migrated all transparent balances to shielded — there is no transparent address option.  Addresses use the `zs1` Sapling format (bech32, 78 chars total), visually identical to Zcash Sapling addresses.

The practices below cover wallet-side hygiene that survives even chain-level shielding — the on-chain payload is private, but what you share off-chain (which addresses you publish, which counterparties you transact with) is what links your {brand} trades together over time.
arrr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Pirate Chain trades on {brand}: chain-level shielded transactions, fresh-address hygiene, and wallet compatibility.
arrr.caveats:
Pirate Chain's chain-level shielding hides sender, recipient, and amount on chain — but it does not erase off-chain linkability.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same `zs1` address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders even though the chain itself reveals nothing.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade (Pirate Chain wallets derive these from your HD seed).
- **Wallet compatibility.**  Not every wallet supports Pirate Chain (the major options are Treasure Chest, Pirate.Black, and Verus-integrated Pirate).  Confirm your counterparty has a compatible wallet before agreeing to a price.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Visual collision with Zcash Sapling addresses.**  Pirate Chain `zs1` addresses look exactly like Zcash `zs1` addresses.  {brand}'s per-asset tab and placeholder disambiguate, but if you copy an address from a different context, confirm it belongs to the chain you intend to send on.

dcr.one_line: Hybrid PoW/PoS cryptocurrency with on-chain governance (Politeia) and opt-in CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) wallet-side mixing.
dcr.intro:
Decred (DCR) launched in 2016 as a hybrid Proof-of-Work + Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency with on-chain governance.  Every block is mined by PoW miners AND voted on by 5 PoS ticket-holders chosen pseudo-randomly from the staking pool — neither group can change the protocol rules unilaterally.  On-chain governance via Politeia lets stakeholders propose, debate, and ratify protocol changes; treasury funds (10% of block reward) flow through community vote.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Decred ships an opt-in CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) mixing protocol integrated into dcrwallet: users can enable mixing in their wallet to break the on-chain transaction graph between deposit and withdrawal, similar in posture to Bitcoin coinjoin or Dash PrivateSend.

The practices below cover wallet-side hygiene to make the most of Decred's privacy features.
dcr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Decred trades on {brand}: hybrid PoW/PoS chain, on-chain governance, opt-in CoinShuffle++ wallet mixing, and fresh-address hygiene.
dcr.caveats:
Decred is transparent at the base layer; mixing is opt-in and wallet-side.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same `Ds` or `Dc` address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade (Decred wallets derive these from your HD seed).
- **Use CSPP mixing if you want transaction-level privacy.**  In dcrwallet enable the "Mix Account" option; deposits flow through CoinShuffle++ rounds with other participants before becoming spendable from your mixed account.  Mixing rounds happen approximately every 20 minutes on mainnet.
- **Wallet compatibility.**  The official wallets are dcrwallet (CLI/headless), Decrediton (GUI), and Cake Wallet (mobile, DCR mode).  Some other wallets support DCR send/receive but not CSPP mixing.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Politeia treasury proposals are public.**  Decred's on-chain governance system shows every proposal, vote, and discussion publicly.  This doesn't affect trading on {brand}, but it's worth knowing if you participate in DCR governance.

sol.one_line: High-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency with Proof-of-History sequencing.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
sol.intro:
Solana (SOL) launched in 2020 as a high-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Validators stake SOL and process blocks in rotation under delegated PoS consensus, with Proof-of-History providing a verifiable sequencing oracle that lets validators reach consensus on transaction ordering without coordination overhead.  The combination achieves transaction throughput several orders of magnitude higher than traditional UTXO chains while remaining decentralized — no central freeze authority controls the chain.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Solana has no native protocol-level mixing protocol.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
sol.meta_description: Privacy practices for Solana trades on {brand}: high-throughput PoS chain, transparent base layer, fresh-address hygiene, native vs wrapped SOL, and RPC provider considerations.
sol.caveats:
Solana is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same Solana address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern Solana wallets (Phantom, Solflare) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Send native SOL, not wrapped SOL.**  Wrapped SOL (wSOL) uses the SPL-token form for DEX interoperability; the mint address `So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112` is the famous wSOL identifier.  {brand} trades use NATIVE SOL transfers — sending wSOL to a SOL receive address requires the recipient to unwrap, which may not happen.
- **Watch for Program-Derived Addresses (PDAs).**  PDAs are off-curve addresses controlled by on-chain programs, not by private keys.  If you send SOL to a PDA, the recipient can't move funds out unless the owning program has a withdraw instruction.  Most wallets show a warning before sending to a PDA; pay attention.
- **Same address shape as USDT-Solana and USDC-Solana.**  A Solana base58 address could be a native SOL account, a USDT-Solana token account, or a USDC-Solana token account — the format is identical.  {brand}'s order asset field tells you which one to send; double-check before signing the transaction in your wallet.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Solana RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an RPC endpoint (Helius, QuickNode, Triton, public mainnet-beta) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting a Solana RPC node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.

eth.one_line: Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency on the Ethereum mainnet.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
eth.intro:
Ethereum (ETH) launched in 2015 as a smart-contract platform.  In September 2022 the chain transitioned from Proof-of-Work to Proof-of-Stake consensus ("The Merge") — validators stake ETH and process blocks in rotation, with no central freeze authority controlling the chain.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Ethereum has no native protocol-level mixing protocol.  Tornado Cash was a notable smart-contract mixer but has been sanctioned in many jurisdictions; {brand} does not recommend or rely on it.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
eth.meta_description: Privacy practices for Ethereum trades on {brand}: PoS chain, transparent base layer, fresh-address hygiene, native vs wrapped ETH, contract-destination warnings, ENS limitations, and RPC provider considerations.
eth.caveats:
Ethereum is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same Ethereum address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern Ethereum wallets (MetaMask, Rabby, Rainbow) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Send native ETH, not wrapped ETH.**  Wrapped ETH (WETH) is an ERC-20 token used for DEX interoperability.  {brand} trades use NATIVE ETH transfers — sending WETH to an ETH receive address requires the recipient to unwrap, which may not happen.
- **Watch for contract destinations.**  Ethereum addresses can be externally-owned accounts (EOAs, controlled by a private key) OR smart contracts.  Sending ETH to a contract without a `payable receive()` or `fallback()` function reverts; the funds aren't lost but the transaction fails and you pay gas.  Most wallets warn before sending to contracts; pay attention.
- **Same address shape as every EVM token-account.**  An Ethereum 0x-address could be a native ETH EOA, a USDT-ERC20 token-account, a USDC-Base token-account, a DAI-Polygon token-account, or any EVM contract.  The format is identical.  {brand}'s order asset field (plus the network field for multi-network assets) tells you which one to send; double-check before signing the transaction in your wallet.
- **ENS names are not resolved.**  Pasting `alice.eth` will fail {brand}'s address validator — paste the raw 0x address.  Resolving ENS would require a centralized RPC dependency that violates Morphit's distributed-no-SPOF design.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Ethereum RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an RPC endpoint (Infura, Alchemy, QuickNode, public mainnet) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting an Ethereum node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.
- **Gas fees can leak timing.**  Ethereum gas prices vary by congestion.  Submitting a transaction during a high-gas window with a higher tip can correlate the tx to a specific time window.  Standard wallet defaults (medium priority) blend with the broader mempool.

xrp.one_line: Federated Byzantine Agreement cryptocurrency on the XRP Ledger.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
xrp.intro:
Ripple (XRP) launched in 2012 as a payment-focused cryptocurrency.  XRPL uses Federated Byzantine Agreement (FBA) consensus — validators on a Unique Node List (UNL) reach agreement on transaction ordering.  The default UNL is published by the XRP Ledger Foundation (non-profit) with the for-profit Ripple Labs Inc. historically influencing validator selection.  Native XRP cannot be frozen by any central authority — the freeze flag on XRPL applies only to issued tokens (IOUs), not to native XRP.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, amount, and destination tag (if present) are all visible on chain like Bitcoin.  XRPL has no native protocol-level mixing.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
xrp.meta_description: Privacy practices for Ripple (XRP) trades on {brand}: XRPL FBA consensus, transparent base layer, destination tag UX, reserve requirement, and RPC provider considerations.
xrp.caveats:
XRPL is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same XRPL address across multiple {brand} listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern XRPL wallets (Xaman, Crossmark, Bifrost) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Destination tags are not a privacy feature — they're an identifier, and {brand} cannot carry one.** A tag is visible on chain and correlates transactions. {brand}'s address share has no tag field and its payment link sets none, so never share an exchange-hosted deposit address that needs a tag (the funds would be lost in the exchange's pool); share a self-custody address that needs no tag.
- **Reserve requirement creates account-creation visibility.**  Your first incoming XRP must be ≥1 XRP (the base reserve).  The on-chain `Payment` transaction that funds a new account is publicly visible as account activation, which is a stronger correlation signal than a regular payment to an already-existing account.  If reducing this signal matters, fund the receive address yourself first (from an account that's already mixed/separated) and only then share it.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **XRPL RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an XRPL RPC endpoint (xrplcluster.com, Ripple's, or a self-hosted rippled node) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting a rippled node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.
- **Consensus-set concentration is a known property.**  The default UNL (Unique Node List) is published by the XRP Ledger Foundation; running your own validator with a custom UNL is supported but uncommon.  For Morphit's purposes this affects censorship-resistance considerations (a coordinated UNL could refuse to include transactions) more than transaction privacy.  Document and decide based on your threat model.
- **Only classic addresses are accepted.** XRPL has a newer "X-address" format (XLS-5d) that bundles a destination tag into the address. {brand} accepts only classic `r`-prefixed addresses and carries no tag, so share a self-custody classic address that needs no tag.

privacy_terms.heading: Privacy & Terms
privacy_terms.privacy_body_1: {brand} runs in your browser. Your keys are generated on your device and never leave it. {brand} does not collect anything about you. Pick a memorable username, that's it.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_2: Every offer you post — along with the feedback and reviews you leave and receive — is public on the blockchain, for reputation-building, posterity, and your own research on other traders.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_protected: By contrast, your chat conversations stay 100% private. Direct messages between traders are end-to-end encrypted — they live on the blockchain only as ciphertext that you and your trade partner can read, never the operator, the indexers, or anyone else watching the chain. {brand} also collects no name, email, phone, or ID, and the payment details you exchange (such as a receiving address) move through that encrypted channel instead of the public orderbook.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_3: We encourage you to use a VPN, Tor, I2P, ENS or Lokinet when accessing {brand} — anything that hides your IP from the server you're talking to is a good idea. We don't fingerprint your browser, we don't profile you, and we explicitly design our defenses against abuse so they don't punish privacy-conscious users. Our rate limits are crude (a handful of signups per user per day) and easily defeated by VPN rotation — that's a conscious tradeoff. We'd rather accept more abuse than make privacy-respecting users feel unwelcome. If a defense would require tracking you to work, we don't ship it.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_zero_clearnet_link: We go further than encouraging privacy.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_zero_clearnet_post: A Morphit node can run with zero use of the clearnet internet: chain reads and software updates travel over Tor and I2P, BTC/XMR fee checks and prices over Tor, and on such a node a firewall lets only Tor and I2P reach the internet. The node claims this only when its own checks pass, and other nodes show it as that instance's own statement, which they cannot verify. It is per-node — a clearnet instance still uses clearnet by design. For someone in a censored region, that is a marketplace node with no clearnet address to block, which visitors reach over Tor or I2P.
privacy_terms.terms_body: Please abide by the Non-Aggression Principle (NAP). Cursing is acceptable, but just keep in mind that there are all ages that use {brand}. Elderly, teens and everyone in between. All OPINIONS are welcome here, but directed insults are not. Your buy/sell orders, your private chats and the feedback section are immutable, so wording is everything. State your opinion, then stop. Don't start fights. Do not post illegal or obviously objectionable stuff. Remember your manners, be nice. 💚💙

run_a_node.title: Run a Morphit node
run_a_node.subtitle_post: . Earn 90% of the BLURT paid listing fees!
run_a_node.why_uncensor_body: Every additional instance makes the network harder to censor. If your country blocks morphit.io, your instance stays reachable. You serve users who'd otherwise have no way to trade.
run_a_node.why_community_body: Brand the interface for your region, your language, your local payment methods. Users trust frontends that speak their language and feel familiar — yours will.
run_a_node.why_privacy_body: Users trading on your instance might share their request-level metadata with your server and not with anyone else. Their public trading activity (orders, encrypted chats, reviews) is on chain so everyone can verify it.
run_a_node.why_privacy_body_2: Encourage users to use a VPN and your (included) Tor and/or I2P addresses. Your alternate, hidden addresses let users reach your instance from jurisdictions where clearnet access is blocked. No SSL/https certificates are needed either and the impact is enormous for users in censored networks and countries.
run_a_node.why_earn_body:
Every BLURT-paid listing fee your instance attracts pays you 90% — only 10% goes to the Morphit treasury to fund development and maintenance of the Morphit software.

No middleman can access your money: each fee is paid as two automated blockchain transfers — 90% straight to your fees account, 10% to the treasury.

Payouts are in BLURT, so if BLURT appreciates, so do your earnings — without any additional work on your part.
run_a_node.step1_title: Get a machine and a web address
run_a_node.step1_body: A cheap VPS or an old PC/laptop running Ubuntu — aim for 4 GB of RAM or more (8 GB is comfy) and 80 GB of disk. A Raspberry Pi 4 works too. Add a domain name (about $10/year) from any registrar and point it at the machine. Hosting from home? No static IP needed — the setup wizard turns on dynamic-DNS for you.
run_a_node.step3_title: Tell the world about your site
run_a_node.step3_body: You instantly appear in the /operators and /instances directories and you start earning the 90% share of the Blurt-paid listing fees on your site automatically. See the operator-earnings FAQ for the economics.
run_a_node.asset_policy_heading: Your instance, your asset and payment-methods policies
run_a_node.asset_policy_body: The federation lets each Operator pick which tradable assets their site supports. You can opt out per-asset and even configure which payment methods your site should support such as Cash, Paypal, Klarna, etc.
run_a_node.asset_policy_federation_body: Disabling an asset on your instance doesn't hide peer instances' orders from your users — chain history is shared, so your orderbook can still show them.
run_a_node.req_hw_value: 2+ CPUs, 4+ GB RAM, 80+ GB drive space (SSD is best)
run_a_node.req_network_value: Home internet works fine — DDNS handles dynamic IPs, no static IP required
run_a_node.req_time_value: Under 15 minutes monthly for checking your relay balance
